introduction:
Marcus Aurelius never meant these notes to be read. He was the most powerful man in the world — emperor of Rome — yet he wrote them at night, on campaign, as private reminders to himself about how to live: with reason, justice, and steadiness in the face of death. That is why the book has no argument and no audience. It is a mind talking to itself.

This Lectio Edition renders his Greek into clear, contemporary English — grounded in the public-domain translations of George Long (1862) and Méric Casaubon (1634) and checked against the original. Read it straight through, or tap any line to compare a historical translation or the Greek.

sections.label: Book I
sections.title: What I Learned, and From Whom

segments.text: From my grandfather Verus, I learned to be good-natured and to keep my temper under control.
From everything I heard and remembered about my father, I learned modesty and a strong, manly character.
From my mother, I learned reverence and generosity; to hold back not only from doing wrong but even from thinking it; and to live simply, far from the habits of the rich.
From my great-grandfather, I learned the value of not relying on public schools but having good teachers at home — and that this is something worth spending freely on.

From my tutor, I learned not to take sides among the racing teams at the Circus or the rival gladiators in the arena; to endure hard work, to want little, to do things with my own hands, to mind my own business, and to refuse to listen to gossip.

From Diognetus, I learned not to waste myself on trivial things; not to believe the claims of magicians and quacks about spells and exorcisms; and not to take up fashionable hobbies like breeding fighting quails. He taught me to put up with plain speaking and to take philosophy seriously; he led me to hear the philosophers Bacchius, Tandasis, and Marcianus, to write dialogues as a boy, and to choose the simple camp-bed and animal skins of the Greek discipline.

From Rusticus, I came to see that my character needed work and discipline. He kept me from chasing clever showmanship, from writing on abstract theories, from delivering little sermons, and from showing off as a model of self-discipline or charity. He taught me to give up ornate rhetoric, poetry, and fine writing; to write plainly, like the simple letter he sent my mother from Sinuessa; to make peace readily with anyone who had wronged me, the moment they were willing; to read closely rather than settle for a superficial grasp; and not to nod along with people who only talk a lot. It was Rusticus who introduced me to Epictetus' teachings, lending me his own copy.

From Apollonius, I learned independence of mind and steady purpose — relying on reason and nothing else, even for a moment — and to stay the same person in sharp pain, in the loss of a child, and in long illness. In him I saw a living example of a man who could be both utterly firm and gentle, never irritable in teaching, who treated his real gift — his skill in explaining philosophy — as the least of his merits. From him I also learned how to accept favors from friends without feeling diminished or letting them pass unacknowledged.

From Sextus, I learned kindness, and the example of a household run the way a good father runs his family; the idea of living in agreement with nature; dignity without pretense; and genuine care for my friends. He bore patiently with ignorant people and with those who hold opinions without thinking them through. He could get along with anyone — his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet people held him in the deepest respect. He had a gift for working out and arranging, clearly and methodically, the principles a life needs. He never showed anger or any other passion; he was at once completely calm and deeply affectionate. He gave praise quietly and carried great learning without ever parading it.

From Alexander the grammarian, I learned not to pounce on mistakes — not to embarrass someone for a slip in grammar or pronunciation, but to work the correct form smoothly into my reply, or by confirming the point, or by some other tactful prompt.
From Fronto, I learned how much envy, cunning, and hypocrisy come with absolute power, and that the people we call aristocrats tend to be rather short on ordinary human warmth.

From Alexander the Platonist, I learned not to say or write to people, often or without real need, that I am 'too busy,' and not to keep dodging my obligations to those around me by always pleading urgent business.

From Catulus, I learned not to brush off a friend's complaint, even an unfair one, but to try to set things right; to speak warmly of my teachers, as people say Domitius and Athenodotus did; and to love my children truly.

From my brother Severus, I learned to love my family, the truth, and justice. Through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, and Brutus; and from him I got the idea of a society governed by one law for all, administered with equal rights and freedom of speech, and of a kingship that values above all the liberty of those it governs. He taught me a steady, undistracted devotion to philosophy; a readiness to do good and to give generously; optimism; and trust that my friends loved me. He never hid what he thought of those he disapproved of, so his friends never had to guess his wishes — it was simply plain.

From Maximus, I learned self-mastery and not to be thrown off course by anything; good cheer in every circumstance, including illness; a character that mixed sweetness with dignity; and doing whatever lay before me without grumbling. Everyone trusted that he meant what he said and acted with good intentions. He was never astonished, never in a hurry, never put things off; he was never at a loss, never downcast, never forced a laugh to cover irritation, and never flew into anger or suspicion. He was generous, forgiving, and honest, and gave the impression of a man who had always been upright rather than one who had had to be corrected. No one could ever feel looked down on by him, or imagine himself the better man — and he had a gift for being agreeably funny.

In my adoptive father, Antoninus, I saw gentleness and an unshakable commitment to decisions made after careful thought. He was indifferent to the so-called honors people crave; he loved hard work and persistence, and was open to anyone with a proposal for the common good. He gave every man exactly what he deserved, and he knew from experience when to press hard and when to ease off. He thought of himself as no more than an ordinary citizen, and he freed his friends from any obligation to dine with him or attend him on his travels; those kept away by other duties always found him unchanged. In council he examined matters carefully and patiently, never breaking off too soon, satisfied with first impressions. He kept his friends without tiring of them and without being extravagantly attached. He was content in every situation, cheerful, and farsighted, attending to the smallest details without fuss. He put a stop to flattery and applause aimed at himself. He watched constantly over what the empire needed, managed its spending well, and patiently bore the criticism this drew. He was neither superstitious toward the gods nor a courter of popular favor; he was sober and steady in everything, never vulgar, never chasing novelty. The comforts that fortune supplied in abundance he used without arrogance and without apology — enjoying them naturally when they were there, and not missing them when they were gone. No one could call him a sophist, a glib servant, or a pedant; everyone recognized him as a mature, complete man, beyond flattery, able to govern himself and others. He honored genuine philosophers and did not reproach the false ones, though he was never taken in by them. He was easy in conversation and charming without being tiresome. He cared for his health sensibly — not clinging to life or fussing over his looks, yet not neglecting himself — so that he rarely needed a doctor. He was quick to make way for those with real talent, in eloquence, law, ethics, or anything else, and helped each win the recognition he deserved. He followed his country's traditions without making a show of it. He disliked change and restlessness, preferring the same places and pursuits, and after his bouts of headache he came back fresh and vigorous to his work. He kept few secrets, and only about public affairs. He was prudent and economical in staging public shows, putting up buildings, and making gifts to the people — a man who looked to what ought to be done, not to the reputation it would earn. He did not bathe at odd hours, did not build for the sake of building, and was indifferent to his food and to the cut and color of his clothes. There was nothing harsh in him, nothing relentless or violent, nothing 'driven to the sweating point'; he examined everything calmly, as if he had all the time in the world — orderly, steady, and consistent. What was said of Socrates fits him: he could go without the things most people cannot do without, and enjoy in moderation the things most people cannot enjoy without overdoing it. To be strong enough for both — to do without, and to enjoy with restraint — is the mark of a man whose soul is balanced and unbeatable, exactly as he showed during Maximus' illness.

To the gods I owe good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, good relatives and friends — almost everything good. I owe it to them, too, that I never lost my temper and wronged any of them, though my nature was such that, given the chance, I might have; by their grace, the circumstances that would have tested me never came together. I am grateful that I was not raised too long by my father's mistress; that I kept my innocence and did not become a man before my time, but if anything waited longer than I needed to. I lived under a ruler and father who stripped away my pride and showed me that one can live in a palace without bodyguards, fine clothes, torches, statues, and such display, and can bring oneself nearly to the level of a private citizen without becoming, for that reason, any smaller in spirit or any slacker in the public duties a ruler must perform. The gods gave me a brother whose character spurred me to watch over myself, and whose respect and affection gladdened me; children who were not born dull or deformed; and the good sense not to get further in rhetoric and poetry and other studies that might have absorbed me had I felt I was excelling. I was quick to give those who raised me the honors they seemed to want, instead of putting them off with promises because they were still young. I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus. I formed clear and frequent pictures of what it means to live according to nature, so that, as far as the gods and their gifts and help and inspiration were concerned, nothing kept me from living that way at once — though I still fall short through my own fault, by not heeding their reminders and almost explicit instructions. My body has held out this long in such a life. I never laid a hand on Benedicta or Theodotus, and when I later fell into infatuations, I recovered. Though I was often annoyed with Rusticus, I never went so far as to do something I would regret. My mother, though fated to die young, spent her last years with me. Whenever I wanted to help someone in need, I was never told there was no money for it — and I myself never had to ask such help from anyone. I have a wife so obedient, affectionate, and unaffected; and I had no shortage of good teachers for my children. Remedies were shown to me in dreams, including ones for spitting blood and for dizziness. And when I was drawn to philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, or waste my time on historical writers, on untangling logical puzzles, or on speculating about the heavens. For all of these, I needed the help of the gods and of fortune.

Begin each morning by telling yourself: today I will meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, envious, and unsociable. They are like this because they cannot tell good from evil. But I have seen that the nature of the good is beautiful and the nature of the bad is ugly, and that the one who does wrong is related to me—not by blood or birth, but because we share the same mind and the same fragment of the divine. So none of them can truly harm me, since no one can force me into anything ugly, and I cannot be angry with a relative or hate him. We were made to work together, like the feet, the hands, the eyelids, the rows of upper and lower teeth. To work against one another, then, is against nature—and resentment and turning away are exactly that.

Whatever I am, I am just a little flesh and breath and the part that governs. Put your books aside; stop letting them distract you—you are not allowed that anymore. Instead, as though you were already dying, look down on the flesh: it is just blood and bones, a mesh of nerves, veins, and arteries. Look at the breath, too, and see what it is—air, never the same, breathed out and sucked back in every moment. The third thing is the governing part. Think of it this way: you are an old man now. Stop letting it be a slave. Stop letting it be jerked around like a puppet by unsociable impulses. Stop being dissatisfied with what the present holds, or flinching from what the future brings.

Everything that comes from the gods is full of providence. Even what comes from chance is not cut off from nature, but woven and tangled together with the things providence arranges. Everything flows from that source. And there is also necessity, and what serves the good of the whole universe, of which you are a part. Whatever the nature of the whole brings is good for each of its parts, and whatever keeps that nature going is good too. The universe is kept alive by the changes of the elements, and also by the changes of the things made from those elements. Let these principles be enough for you; hold them always as settled convictions. And throw away your thirst for books, so that you do not die complaining, but cheerfully, sincerely, and truly grateful to the gods from your heart.

Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many chances the gods have given you that you still do not use. It is time, at last, to grasp what universe you are part of, and that your existence flows from the one who administers that universe, and that a limit has been set on your time. If you do not use that time to clear the clouds from your mind, it will pass—and you will pass with it—and it will never come back.

Every moment, set yourself firmly, as a Roman and a man, to do the task in front of you with perfect and simple dignity, with affection, freedom, and justice, and to free yourself from every other thought. You will free yourself if you do each act of your life as if it were your last—setting aside all carelessness, all passionate resistance to what reason commands, all hypocrisy, all self-love, and all discontent with the lot you have been given. See how few things a man needs to master in order to live a calm life, like the life of the gods; for the gods themselves will ask nothing more from anyone who keeps to these things.

You wrong yourself, you wrong yourself, my soul—and soon you will no longer have the chance to honor yourself. Every person gets just one life, and yours is nearly over, yet you still do not respect yourself; instead you stake your happiness on the souls of other people.

Do the things happening around you pull you in every direction? Then give yourself time to learn something new and good, and stop spinning. But beware of being swept off in the other direction too; for those who wear themselves out with constant activity are just as foolish if they have no goal to aim every action—and indeed every thought—toward.
A man is rarely seen to be unhappy because he failed to notice what was in someone else's mind; but those who fail to watch the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy.

Always keep this in mind: what the nature of the whole is, what my own nature is, how mine relates to the whole, what kind of part it is and of what kind of whole—and that no one can stop you from always acting and speaking in keeping with the nature you are part of.

When Theophrastus compares wrongdoings—the kind of comparison one would make according to ordinary human ideas—he says, like a true philosopher, that offenses committed out of desire are more blameworthy than those committed out of anger. For the man stirred by anger seems to turn away from reason with a kind of pain and an unwilling flinch; but the man who offends out of desire is overcome by pleasure and seems somehow more lacking in self-control, more weak-willed in his wrongdoing. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the offense committed with pleasure deserves more blame than the one committed with pain. On the whole, the angry man is like someone who was first wronged and is driven by pain into anger, while the other moves on his own impulse to do wrong, carried into action by desire.

Since it is possible that you may leave this life at any moment, govern every action and thought accordingly. As for leaving the company of people, if there are gods, there is nothing to fear—they will not let you fall into evil. And if there are no gods, or if they take no interest in human affairs, then why would I want to live in a universe with no gods and no providence? But in truth they do exist, and they do care about human things, and they have placed everything within a man's power so that he need not fall into real evils. As for anything else, if it were truly evil, they would have arranged that too, so that it would be entirely in a man's power to avoid it. And anything that does not make a man worse—how could it make his life worse? It is not possible that the nature of the universe overlooked these things out of ignorance, nor out of knowing them while lacking the power to guard against or correct them. Nor is it possible that it made so great a mistake, through weakness or lack of skill, that good and evil should fall on the good and the bad alike. But death and life, honor and dishonor, pain and pleasure—all of these come equally to good men and bad, and they make us neither better nor worse. So they are neither good nor evil.

How quickly everything vanishes—the bodies themselves into the universe, and the memory of them into time. Consider the nature of all the things we sense, especially those that lure us with the bait of pleasure, or terrify us with pain, or are trumpeted about by empty fame: how worthless, contemptible, shabby, perishable, and dead they are. It is the work of the mind to observe all this—to observe, too, who these people really are whose opinions and voices grant reputation, and what death is. If a man looks at death by itself, and uses reflection to strip away everything the imagination piles onto it, he will see it as nothing more than a process of nature; and to be afraid of a process of nature is childish. And death is not only a process of nature, but something that serves nature's purposes. Observe, too, how man draws near to the divine, by what part of himself, and when that part is rightly disposed.

Nothing is more pitiable than a man who circles around everything, prying into what lies beneath the earth, as the poet says, and trying to guess by conjecture what is in his neighbors' minds, never realizing that it is enough to attend to the spirit within himself and to revere it sincerely. To revere that spirit means keeping it free from passion and thoughtlessness, and from discontent with what comes from gods and men. What comes from the gods deserves reverence for its excellence; what comes from men should be dear to us because they are our kin—and sometimes, in a way, they even move us to pity because they do not know good from bad, a defect no smaller than the one that robs a person of the power to tell white from black.

Even if you were going to live for three thousand years, or ten thousand times that long, still remember this: no one loses any life but the one he is living now, and no one lives any life but the one he is losing now. So the longest life and the shortest come to the same thing. The present moment is the same for everyone, even though what is passing away is not the same for each; and so what is lost turns out to be only a moment. For a man cannot lose either the past or the future—how can anyone take from him what he does not have? Keep two things in mind, then. First, that all things from eternity have the same forms and come round again in a circle, so it makes no difference whether a man sees the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or forever. Second, that the longest-lived man and the one who dies soonest lose exactly the same. For the present is the only thing a man can be deprived of, since it is the only thing he has—and a man cannot lose what he does not have.
Remember that everything is a matter of opinion. The saying of Monimus the Cynic makes this plain, and the use of it is plain too, if a man takes from it as much as is true.

The soul of a man does violence to itself, first of all, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess or a kind of tumor on the universe. For to be vexed at anything that happens is to cut yourself off from nature, which contains the natures of all other things in its various parts. Second, the soul does violence to itself when it turns away from another person, or moves toward him meaning to do harm, as the souls of angry people do. Third, when it is overpowered by pleasure or pain. Fourth, when it puts on an act, doing or saying anything insincerely or untruthfully. Fifth, when it lets any of its own acts or impulses have no aim, doing things thoughtlessly without considering what they are—when even the smallest things ought to be done with an end in view; and the end of rational beings is to follow the reason and the law of the most ancient city and commonwealth.

In human life, time is a mere point, the substance is in constant flux, perception is dim, the whole body is matter bound to rot, the soul is a whirl, fortune is hard to predict, and fame is mindless. In a word, everything of the body is a flowing stream, everything of the soul is dream and vapor, life is a war and a stranger's brief stay, and lasting fame is oblivion. What, then, can guide a man? One thing, and one thing only: philosophy. And this means keeping the spirit within him free from violence and unharmed, above pleasures and pains, doing nothing without a purpose and nothing falsely or with pretense, not depending on whether another man does or does not do something; and besides this, accepting everything that happens and everything allotted to him as coming from wherever he himself came; and, finally, awaiting death with a cheerful mind, since it is nothing but the breaking up of the elements that make up every living being. But if it does no harm to the elements themselves to be continually changing one into another, why should a man dread the change and dissolution of them all? It is in keeping with nature, and nothing that is in keeping with nature is evil.

We should keep in mind not only that our life is wearing away day by day, with less and less of it left, but also this: even if we live longer, there is no guarantee that the mind will stay sharp enough to understand things and keep the power of reflection that strives to grasp what is divine and what is human. For once a person slips into senility, the breathing and digestion and imagination and appetite and all the rest will keep working, but the power to make full use of ourselves, to fulfill our duty completely, to sort out every impression clearly, to judge whether the time has come to leave life, and everything else that requires a trained reason, all of that is already extinguished. So we must hurry, not only because we draw closer to death every day, but because the grasp and understanding of things gives out first.

We should also notice that even the byproducts of natural processes have a certain charm and attractiveness. When bread is baked, for instance, some parts crack open at the surface, and these cracks, though they happen contrary to the baker's intention, are beautiful in their own way and somehow whet the appetite. Likewise figs split open when fully ripe; and in ripe olives the very nearness to rotting lends the fruit a peculiar beauty. The drooping ears of grain, the lion's brow, the foam dripping from a wild boar's mouth, and many other things, though far from beautiful if you examine them on their own, still add to the charm of the natural things they accompany and please the mind. So anyone with real feeling and deeper insight into what is produced in the universe will find that scarcely one of these secondary effects fails to seem pleasingly arranged. He will look at the actual gaping jaws of wild beasts with no less pleasure than at those painters and sculptors imitate; he will see in an old woman and an old man a kind of ripeness and grace; and he will be able to look on the appealing loveliness of the young with chaste eyes. Many such things will present themselves, pleasing not to everyone, but only to the person who has become truly familiar with Nature and her works.

Hippocrates cured many diseases, then fell sick and died himself. The Chaldean astrologers foretold the deaths of many, and then fate caught up with them too. Alexander, Pompey, and Gaius Caesar, after wiping out whole cities again and again and cutting to pieces tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry in battle, themselves at last departed from life. Heraclitus, after all his theories about the universe going up in flames, filled up with water inside and died smeared all over with mud. Lice killed Democritus, and other vermin killed Socrates. What does all this mean? You boarded the ship, you made the voyage, you have reached shore: get off. If it is to another life, there is no lack of gods even there; and if it is to a state without sensation, you will no longer be held by pains and pleasures, no longer a slave to this vessel, the body, which is as far inferior to what it serves as a servant is to its master. For the one is intelligence and divinity, the other is earth and decay.

Do not waste what remains of your life in thoughts about other people, unless you are relating those thoughts to some common good. For you lose the chance to do something else when you let your mind run on things like this: what is so-and-so doing, and why, and what is he saying, and what is he thinking, and what is he scheming, and everything of that kind that pulls you away from watching your own ruling power. So in the run of your thoughts you should cut out everything aimless and useless, and above all the over-curious and the spiteful. Train yourself to think only of things such that, if someone suddenly asked you, 'What are you thinking about right now?', you could answer at once and openly, 'This' or 'That', and it would be plain from your words that everything in you is straightforward and kind, the thoughts of a social creature, one with no concern for pleasure or sensual indulgence at all, no rivalry, no envy, no suspicion, nothing you would blush to admit was on your mind. A person like this, who no longer puts off being among the best, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods, using too the divinity seated within him, which keeps a man uncontaminated by pleasure, unhurt by any pain, untouched by any insult, immune to wrong, a fighter in the noblest of fights, one who cannot be overpowered by any passion, steeped deep in justice, welcoming with his whole soul everything that happens and is assigned to him as his share. He rarely, and only out of great necessity and for the common good, lets himself imagine what someone else is saying or doing or thinking. He takes only what is his own as the material for his action; he keeps in mind what has been allotted to him out of the sum of things; he makes his own conduct fair; and he is convinced that his own portion is good. For the lot assigned to each person is carried along with him and carries him along with it. He also remembers that every rational being is his kin, that caring for all people is in keeping with human nature, and that he should hold on to the opinions not of everyone, but only of those who admittedly live according to nature. As for those who do not live so, he keeps in mind what sort of people they are at home and abroad, by night and by day, and what they are, and with what company they lead their impure lives. So he sets no value at all on the praise of such men, since they are not even satisfied with themselves.

Do not work unwillingly, nor without regard for the common good, nor without careful thought, nor in a distracted way. Do not dress up your thoughts with studied ornament. Do not be a man of many words or one who busies himself with too many things. And further, let the divinity within you be the guardian of a being who is manly and mature, engaged in public affairs, a Roman, and a ruler, one who has taken up his post like a man waiting for the signal that calls him out of life, ready to go, needing no oath and no one else's testimony. Be cheerful, too, and do not look outside yourself for help or for the peace of mind that others give. A man should stand upright on his own, not be propped up by others.

If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, and courage; in short, anything better than your own mind's contentment in the things it lets you do according to right reason, and in your contentment with the lot assigned to you without your own choosing; if, I say, you see anything better than this, then turn to it with all your soul and enjoy what you have found to be best. But if nothing appears better than the divinity planted within you, which has brought all your appetites under its control, which scrutinizes every impression, which has, as Socrates said, detached itself from the persuasions of the senses, submitted itself to the gods, and made the welfare of mankind its care; if you find everything else smaller and of less worth than this, then give way to nothing else. For once you swerve and lean toward something else, you will no longer be able, without distraction, to give first place to that good thing that is properly and uniquely your own. It is not right that anything of a different kind, such as the praise of the crowd, or power, or the enjoyment of pleasure, should compete with what is good in the rational and social sense. All these things, even if they seem to fit in only slightly, suddenly gain the upper hand and sweep us away. So you, I say, must simply and freely choose the better and hold to it. But the useful is the better. Well then, if it is useful to you as a rational being, keep to it; but if it is useful only to you as an animal, say so, and hold to your judgment without arrogance, only taking care to make the inquiry by a sound method.

Never value as good for yourself anything that would force you to break a promise, to lose your self-respect, to hate anyone, to grow suspicious, to curse, to play the hypocrite, or to crave anything that needs walls and curtains to hide it. The man who has put his own intelligence and inner divinity, and the honoring of its excellence, above everything else plays no tragic role, does not groan, and will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Best of all, he will live without either chasing death or running from it. Whether his soul is to be enclosed in the body for a longer or a shorter time makes no difference to him at all; even if he must depart at once, he will go as readily as if turning to any other task that can be done decently and in order, caring all through life about only this: that his mind never turns away from anything that belongs to a thinking creature and a member of a community.

In the mind of a man who has been disciplined and purified you will find nothing rotten, no foulness, no sore merely scabbed over. Fate does not catch his life unfinished, as one might say of an actor who leaves the stage before the play is over and done. And there is nothing in him servile, nothing affected, nothing too tightly bound to other things nor yet cut off from them, nothing that deserves blame, nothing that looks for a place to hide.

Revere the faculty that forms opinions. Everything depends on it, whether or not there will arise in your ruling part any opinion out of keeping with nature and the constitution of a rational being. This faculty promises freedom from hasty judgment, friendship toward others, and obedience to the gods.

So throw everything else away and hold on to these few things only. And remember as well that each of us lives only in the present moment, this indivisible point of time, and that all the rest of our life is either past or uncertain. Short, then, is the time anyone lives, and small the corner of the earth where he lives, and short too the longest fame after death, kept alive only by a succession of poor mortals who will die very soon themselves, and who do not even know their own selves, much less someone who died long ago.

To the aids already mentioned let this one be added: make for yourself a definition or description of whatever is presented to you, so that you can see clearly what kind of thing it is in its essence, stripped bare, in its full reality, and can name it properly, and name the parts of which it is composed and into which it will dissolve. Nothing lifts the mind so much as being able to examine, methodically and truthfully, every object that comes up in life, and always to look at things in such a way as to see at the same time what kind of universe this is, what purpose each thing serves in it, what value it has in relation to the whole and what value in relation to man, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are like households. Ask what each thing is, what it is made of, how long it is in its nature to last, this thing that now makes an impression on me, and what virtue I need to meet it, such as gentleness, courage, truthfulness, loyalty, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest. So on every occasion a man should say: this comes from god; and this comes by the apportioning and spinning of the thread of destiny, by such coincidence and chance; and this comes from one of my own kind, a kinsman and partner, who does not know, however, what accords with his nature. But I know; and for that reason I treat him, according to the natural law of fellowship, with kindness and justice. At the same time, in things that are neither good nor bad, I try to gauge the worth of each.

If you work at the task before you, following right reason in earnest, with vigor and calm, letting nothing else distract you, but keeping your divine part pure as though you might have to give it back at any moment; if you hold to this, expecting nothing, fearing nothing, but content with your present activity in accordance with nature, and with heroic truthfulness in every word and sound you utter, then you will live happily. And there is no one who can stop you.

Just as doctors always keep their instruments and scalpels ready for cases that suddenly call for their skill, so you should keep your principles ready for understanding things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, mindful of the bond that links the divine and the human to each other. For you will do nothing well in human affairs without at the same time keeping the divine in view, and nothing well in divine affairs without keeping the human in view.

Do not drift aimlessly any longer. You are not going to read your own notebooks now, nor the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks, nor the selections from books you were saving up for old age. So hurry to the goal before you, throw away idle hopes, and come to your own rescue, if you care about yourself at all, while it is still in your power.

People do not realize how many things are meant by the words stealing, sowing, buying, keeping quiet, seeing what ought to be done; for this last is not done with the eyes but by another kind of sight.

Body, soul, intelligence: to the body belong sensations, to the soul appetites, to the intelligence principles. To receive impressions of forms through appearances belongs even to animals. To be jerked about by the strings of desire belongs both to wild beasts and to men who have turned themselves into women, and to a Phalaris and a Nero. And to have the intelligence that points the way to what seems fitting belongs even to those who do not believe in the gods, who betray their country, and who do their foul deeds behind shut doors. If, then, everything else is shared by all those I have mentioned, what remains as peculiar to the good man is this: to be pleased and content with whatever happens, and with the thread spun for him; not to defile the divinity seated in his breast nor disturb it with a crowd of images, but to keep it serene, following it obediently as a god, never saying anything contrary to the truth nor doing anything contrary to justice. And if everyone refuses to believe that he lives a simple, modest, and contented life, he is not angry with any of them, nor does he stray from the road that leads to the end of life, to which a man ought to come pure, tranquil, ready to depart, and without compulsion perfectly reconciled to his lot.

The part of us that rules from within, when it is in accord with nature, takes whatever happens so readily that it always adapts itself to whatever is possible and is set before it. It needs no particular material to work with; it moves toward its purpose, though under certain conditions, and it turns whatever opposes it into material for itself, the way a fire seizes what falls into it. A small flame would be smothered, but a strong fire quickly takes hold of whatever is piled onto it, consumes it, and rises higher because of that very fuel.
Let nothing be done without a purpose, and nothing except according to the perfect principles of the craft.

People look for places to get away to: country houses, beaches, mountains. You too long for such things very much. But this is the mark of the most ordinary kind of person, since it is in your power, whenever you choose, to retreat into yourself. Nowhere can you find a more peaceful or untroubled retreat than in your own soul, especially when you have within you the kind of thoughts that, by simply looking into them, put you at once into complete tranquillity. And by tranquillity I mean nothing other than a well-ordered mind. So give yourself this retreat constantly, and renew yourself. Keep your principles brief and basic, so that the moment you turn to them they are enough to wash the soul clean and send you back free of all discontent with the things you are returning to. For what is it you are discontented with? With people's wickedness? Then call to mind the conclusion that rational beings exist for one another, that patience is a part of justice, and that people do wrong without meaning to. Consider how many, after their mutual hostility, suspicion, hatred, and fighting, have been laid out dead and reduced to ashes; and be at peace at last. Or perhaps you are dissatisfied with the portion the universe has assigned you. Then recall the alternative: either there is providence, or there are only atoms, a chance jumble of things; or remember the arguments that have proved the world to be a kind of political community; and be at peace at last. Or perhaps bodily things still take hold of you. Then consider further that the mind does not mingle with the breath, whether it moves gently or violently, once it has drawn itself apart and discovered its own power; and remember all you have heard and agreed to about pain and pleasure; and be at peace at last. Or perhaps the desire for what is called fame will torment you. Then see how quickly everything is forgotten; look at the chaos of infinite time on either side of the present, at the emptiness of applause, at the fickleness and poor judgment of those who pretend to give praise, and at the narrowness of the space within which praise is confined. For the whole earth is a mere point, and how tiny a corner of it is this home of yours, and how few people are in it, and what kind of people are those who will praise you.

This, then, is what remains: remember to retreat into this little domain of your own, and above all do not strain or distract yourself, but stay free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. Among the things readiest at hand, to which you should turn, let there be these two. The first is that things do not touch the soul; they stand outside it, unmoving, and our disturbances come only from the opinion within us. The second is that all the things you see are changing this very moment and will soon be no more; keep constantly in mind how many such changes you have already witnessed. The universe is transformation; life is opinion.

If the thinking part of us is shared, then so is the reason that makes us rational beings. If that is so, then the reason which commands us what to do and what not to do is also shared. If that is so, there is a common law as well. If that is so, we are fellow citizens. If that is so, we are members of some political community. If that is so, the world is in a way a state. For what other common community could anyone claim that the whole human race belongs to? And it is from this common community that our very power of thought, our reasoning, and our capacity for law come; or where else would they come from? Just as my earthly part is a portion given to me from a certain earth, my watery part from another element, and my hot, fiery part from some particular source (for nothing comes out of nothing, just as nothing returns to non-existence), so too the thinking part comes from some source.

Death is like birth, a mystery of nature: a combining of the same elements and a dissolving back into the same. It is nothing anyone should be ashamed of, for it is not contrary to the nature of a reasoning creature, nor contrary to the design of our constitution.

It is natural that such things should be done by such people; it is inevitable. If a man refuses to allow it, he might as well refuse to let the fig tree have its juice. By all means keep this in mind: within a very short time both you and he will be dead, and soon not even your names will remain.
Take away your opinion, and you take away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm itself is gone.
Whatever does not make a man worse than he was also does not make his life worse, and does not harm him, either from outside or from within.
The nature of what is universally useful has been compelled to act this way.

Consider that everything which happens, happens justly, and if you observe carefully you will find this to be so. I do not mean merely with respect to the orderly sequence of events, but with respect to justice, as though done by someone who assigns to each thing its due. So keep observing as you have begun, and whatever you do, do it together with this aim: being good, in the sense in which a man is properly understood to be good. Hold to this in every action.
Do not take the same view of things that the person who wrongs you holds, or the view he wishes you to hold; but look at them as they truly are.

A man should always keep these two rules ready at hand. The first is to do only what the reason of the ruling and law-giving faculty suggests for the benefit of people. The second is to change your opinion if someone is at hand to set you right and move you from a mistaken view. But this change of mind must come only from a genuine conviction, of what is just or for the common good or the like, not because it seems pleasant or brings you a good reputation.
Do you have reason? I do. Then why not use it? For if reason does its own work, what more could you want?
You have existed as a part of the whole. You will disappear back into what produced you; or rather, you will be taken back, through transformation, into its generative principle.
Many grains of incense fall on the same altar; one falls sooner, another later, but it makes no difference.
Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people who now regard you as a beast and an ape, if you will return to your principles and to the worship of reason.
Do not act as though you were going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you are alive, while it is still in your power, be good.

How much trouble a man avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he himself does, that it may be just and pure. As Agathon says, do not glance around at the corrupt characters of others, but run straight along the line without swerving from it.

The man who has a fierce desire for fame after death does not consider that every one of those who remember him will himself soon die, and then those who succeed them, until the whole memory of him is snuffed out as it passes through people who admire foolishly and then perish. But suppose that those who remember you were even immortal, and the memory itself immortal: what is that to you? And I do not even ask what it is to the dead, but what it is to the living. What is praise, except so far as it has some practical use? For now you are unreasonably rejecting the gift of nature, clinging instead to something else.

Everything that is in any way beautiful is beautiful in itself and complete in itself; praise is no part of it. Being praised makes a thing neither worse nor better. I say this even of the things commonly called beautiful, such as material objects and works of art. What is truly beautiful needs nothing beyond itself, no more than law does, or truth, or kindness, or modesty. Which of these is made beautiful by being praised, or spoiled by being blamed? Is an emerald made worse than it was if no one praises it? Or gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a shrub?

If souls continue to exist, how does the air contain them from all eternity? But then how does the earth contain the bodies of those buried so long ago? For just as here the change of these bodies, after lasting however long, and their dissolution, make room for other dead bodies, so the souls that pass into the air, after lasting some time, are transformed and dispersed, and take on a fiery nature as they are received back into the generative intelligence of the universe, and in this way make room for fresh souls coming to dwell there. This is the answer a man might give on the assumption that souls continue to exist. But we must think not only of the number of bodies that are buried, but also of the number of animals eaten each day by us and by other animals. What a multitude is consumed, and in a way buried in the bodies of those who feed on them! And yet the earth still receives them, through their changes into blood and their transformations into the airy or the fiery element.
What is the way to investigate the truth here? To divide a thing into what is material and what is the cause of its form.
Do not be spun about, but in every impulse have regard for justice, and at every impression preserve the power of clear understanding.

Everything that is in harmony with you, O Universe, is in harmony with me. Nothing is too early or too late for me that is in due time for you. Everything is fruit to me that your seasons bring, O Nature. From you are all things, in you are all things, to you all things return. The poet says, "Dear city of Cecrops"; will you not say, "Dear city of Zeus"?

Keep yourself occupied with few things, the philosopher says, if you would be tranquil. But consider whether it might not be better to say: do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a creature naturally social requires, and as it requires. For this brings not only the tranquillity that comes from acting well, but also the tranquillity that comes from doing few things. Since the greater part of what we say and do is unnecessary, a man who strips that away will have more leisure and less disquiet. So on every occasion a man should ask himself: is this one of the unnecessary things? And he should strip away not only unnecessary actions but also unnecessary thoughts, so that superfluous actions will not follow from them.
Try out how the life of a good man suits you, the man who is satisfied with the portion assigned to him out of the whole, and satisfied with his own just acts and kindly disposition.

Have you seen those things? Now look at these as well. Do not disturb yourself. Make yourself entirely simple. Does someone do wrong? It is to himself that he does the wrong. Has something happened to you? Very well; out of the universe, from the beginning, everything that happens has been apportioned and spun out for you. In short, your life is brief. You must turn the present to good account with the help of reason and justice. Be sober even in your relaxation.

Either this is a well-ordered universe, or it is a chaos thrown together; but a universe even so. Can there be order within you, yet disorder in the whole? And this when all things are so distinct, so spread out, and yet bound together in sympathy?
A black character, an unmanly one, a stubborn one, brutish, childish, animal, stupid, fraudulent, vulgar, deceitful, tyrannical.

If a man is a stranger to the universe because he does not know what is in it, he is no less a stranger because he does not know what is going on in it. He is a runaway who flees from the social reason. He is blind who shuts the eyes of his understanding. He is poor who has need of another and does not have within himself all that is useful for life. He is an abscess on the universe who withdraws and cuts himself off from the reason of our common nature out of displeasure with what happens, for the same nature that produces these things also produced you. He is a fragment torn from the state who tears his own soul away from the soul of reasoning beings, which is one.

One philosopher is without a tunic, another without a book; here is yet another half naked. "I have no bread," he says, "and still I hold to reason"; and I get no living from my learning, yet still I hold to my reason.

Love the craft you have learned, humble as it may be, and be content with it; and live out the rest of your life as one who has entrusted all that he has to the gods with his whole soul, making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.

Consider, for instance, the times of Vespasian. You will see all the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling sick, dying, making war, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, stubbornly arrogant, suspicious, scheming, wishing some people dead, grumbling about the present, in love, hoarding treasure, craving a consulship, craving royal power. Well, that life of theirs no longer exists at all. Move on to the times of Trajan. Again, everything is the same; their life too is gone. In the same way look at the other ages of time and whole nations, and see how many, after great efforts, soon fell and dissolved into the elements. Above all you should think of those you have known yourself who wore themselves out over trivial things and neglected to do what their own nature required, to hold firmly to that and be content with it. And here you must remember that the attention given to each thing has its proper value and proportion. For thus you will not be dissatisfied, if you give to lesser matters no more attention than is fitting.

The words that were once familiar are now obsolete; and so too the names of those famous in old times are now in a way obsolete: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus, and a little later Scipio and Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian and Antoninus. For all things soon pass away and become a mere story, and complete oblivion soon buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some remarkable way. As for the rest, the moment they have breathed their last they are gone, and no one speaks of them. And to settle the matter, what even is an eternal memory? Nothing at all. What, then, is it that we ought to spend our serious effort on? This one thing: just thoughts, actions that serve the common good, words that never lie, and a disposition that gladly welcomes everything that happens, as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from a source and principle of the same kind.
Willingly give yourself up to Clotho, one of the Fates, and let her spin your thread into whatever she pleases.
Everything lasts only for a day, both the one who remembers and the thing remembered.

Observe constantly that all things come to pass through change, and train yourself to consider that the nature of the universe loves nothing so much as to change what exists and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will come from it. But you think only of seeds cast into the earth or the womb; that is a very crude notion.

You will soon die, and you are still not simple, still not free of disturbances, still not without the suspicion that external things can harm you, still not kindly toward everyone, nor do you yet locate wisdom solely in acting justly.
Examine the ruling principles of people, even of the wise: what kinds of things they avoid, and what kinds they pursue.

What is evil for you does not reside in the ruling principle of another, nor in any change or alteration of your bodily covering. Where, then, is it? It is in that part of you which has the power to form opinions about evils. So let this power form no such opinions, and all is well. Even if what lies nearest to it, the poor body, is cut, burned, festering with pus and rot, still let the part that forms opinions about these things stay quiet; that is, let it judge that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to a bad man and a good one. For whatever happens equally to the man who lives contrary to nature and to the man who lives according to nature is neither according to nature nor contrary to it.

Constantly regard the universe as one living being, with one substance and one soul. Observe how all things refer back to its single awareness; how all things act with one impulse; how all things are co-operating causes of everything that exists; and observe too the continuous spinning of the thread and the weaving of the web.
You are a little soul carrying around a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
It is no evil for things to undergo change, and no good for things to come into being as a result of change.
Time is like a river of all that happens, a violent current; for no sooner has a thing come into view than it is swept away, and another takes its place, and that too will be swept away.

Everything that happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and the fruit in summer; for such are disease and death and slander and treachery and everything else that delights or vexes fools.

In the sequence of things, what comes after always fits aptly with what has gone before; for this sequence is not like a mere list of disconnected items joined only by necessity, but a rational connection. And just as all existing things are arranged together in harmony, so the things that come into being show no mere succession but a certain wonderful kinship.

Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, the death of water to become air, the death of air to become fire, and so on in reverse. Think too of the man who forgets where the road leads, and how people quarrel with the very thing they are in most constant communion with, the reason that governs the universe; and how the things they meet with every day seem strange to them. Consider that we ought not to act and speak as though we were asleep, for even in sleep we seem to act and speak; and that we ought not to act and speak merely as we have been taught, like children repeating what they learned from their parents.

If some god told you that you would die tomorrow, or certainly the day after, you would not care much whether it was the third day or tomorrow, unless you were utterly small-minded, for how slight the difference is. So think it no great matter to die after as many years as you can name rather than tomorrow.

Think continually how many physicians are dead, after so often knitting their brows over the sick; how many astrologers, after predicting other people's deaths with great pretension; how many philosophers, after endless discourses on death and immortality; how many warriors, after killing thousands; how many tyrants, who wielded their power over men's lives with terrible arrogance, as though they were immortal. Think how many whole cities have died, so to speak, Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others. Add to the count all whom you yourself have known, one after another. One man, after burying another, is laid out dead, and another buries him; and all this in a short time. In a word, always observe how fleeting and worthless human things are: what was a little mucus yesterday will be a mummy or ashes tomorrow. So pass through this small span of time in agreement with nature, and end your journey content, as an olive falls when it is ripe, blessing the nature that produced it and giving thanks to the tree on which it grew.
Be like the headland on which the waves break again and again, while it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.

"How unlucky I am, that this has happened to me." Not so; rather, "How lucky I am that, though this has happened to me, I remain free of pain, neither crushed by the present nor afraid of the future." For such a thing might have happened to anyone, but not everyone would have remained free of pain through it. So why call that a misfortune rather than calling this a good fortune? And do you in general call something a man's misfortune when it is not a departure from man's nature? And does a thing seem to you a departure from man's nature when it is not contrary to the will of that nature? Well, you know the will of nature. Will this thing that has happened keep you from being just, great-souled, temperate, prudent, free from rash opinions and falsehood? Will it keep you from being modest, free, and from having everything else by whose presence a man's nature obtains all that is its own? Remember, then, on every occasion that leads you to distress, to apply this principle: this is not a misfortune, but to bear it nobly is good fortune.

It is a common but still a useful aid toward despising death to review those who have clung tenaciously to life. What more have they gained than those who died early? At any rate they lie in their tombs somewhere at last, Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or anyone else like them, men who carried out many others to be buried and were then carried out themselves. The interval between birth and death is small in any case; and consider with how much trouble, in what company, and in what a feeble body it is laboriously passed. So do not regard life as a thing of any great value. Look at the vast stretch of time behind you, and at the time before you, another boundless expanse. In this infinity, what difference is there between the man who lives three days and the man who lives three generations?

Always take the short road, and the short road is the natural one. So say and do everything in keeping with the soundest reason. For such a purpose frees a man from troubles, from struggle, and from all scheming and showy display.

When you wake reluctantly in the morning, keep this thought ready: I am rising to do the work of a human being. Why should I be unhappy, if I am going to do the very things I exist for, the things I was brought into the world to do? Or was I made for this, to lie under the blankets and keep myself warm? But this is more pleasant. So were you made to take your pleasure, and not at all for action and effort? Don't you see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees all working together to put their own parts of the universe in order? And you are unwilling to do the work of a human being, and don't hurry to do what your own nature calls for? But I need rest too. You do. Yet nature has set limits to that, just as she has set limits to eating and drinking; and still you go past those limits, past what is enough, while in your work you do the opposite and stop short of what you could do. So you don't really love yourself, for if you did, you would love your nature and what it wants. People who love their crafts wear themselves out working at them, forgetting to wash or eat; but you value your own nature less than the metalworker values his craft, or the dancer his dancing, or the money-lover his money, or the vain man his scrap of glory. When such people are gripped by a passion for something, they would rather not eat or sleep than fall short of perfecting what they care about. Are the acts that serve society so worthless in your eyes, so much less worthy of your effort?
How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troubling or out of place, and at once to be completely at peace.

Judge that every word and action which is in keeping with nature is fitting for you, and don't be turned aside by the blame that may follow from others, or by their talk. If a thing is good to do or say, don't consider it beneath you. Those people have their own guiding principle and follow their own impulse; pay no attention to that, but go straight ahead, following your own nature and the common nature, for the path of both is one and the same.

I make my way through the things that happen according to nature until I fall and come to rest, breathing out my breath into the same element I draw it from each day, and falling onto the same earth from which my father gathered the seed, my mother the blood, and my nurse the milk; the earth that for so many years has supplied me with food and drink, and that bears me up as I tread on it and put it to so many uses.

You say men cannot admire the sharpness of your wit. So be it. But there are many other qualities about which you cannot say, I am not formed by nature for them. So display those qualities that are entirely within your power: sincerity, dignity, endurance of hard work, indifference to pleasure, contentment with your lot and with little, kindness, frankness, no taste for excess, no triviality, greatness of soul. Don't you see how many qualities you could show right now, for which there is no excuse of natural incapacity or unfitness, and yet you still choose to stay below the mark? Or are you forced by some defect of nature to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to fawn on people, to make a great show of yourself, and to be so restless in your mind? No, by the gods, you could have been free of all this long ago. If you can truly be charged only with being somewhat slow and dull in understanding, then work at this too, instead of neglecting it or taking comfort in your dullness.

One man, when he has done another a service, is quick to put it on the books as a favor owed to him. Another doesn't go that far, but still privately counts the man as his debtor and is well aware of what he has done. A third, in a way, isn't even aware of what he has done; he is like a vine that has produced grapes and looks for nothing more once it has yielded its proper fruit. As a horse runs, a dog tracks game, a bee makes honey, so a man who has done a good deed doesn't call out for others to come and see, but moves on to the next deed, as the vine moves on to bear grapes again in season. So must a person be one of those who act this way without taking notice of it? Yes. But surely it is necessary to be aware of what one is doing, for it is said to be the mark of the social creature to perceive that it is acting for society, and indeed to want its fellow to perceive it too. What you say is true, but you misunderstand the point being made, and for that very reason you will become one of those I described earlier, for even they are led astray by a certain show of reason. But if you will choose to grasp the real meaning of what is said, don't be afraid that you will therefore neglect any social act.
A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the plowed fields and plains of the Athenians. In truth, either we should not pray at all, or we should pray in just this simple and noble way.

Just as we understand what it means when we say that Asclepius prescribed for a man horseback riding, or cold baths, or going barefoot, so we must understand it when we say that the nature of the universe prescribed for a man disease, or loss of a limb, or loss of something, or anything else of the kind. In the first case, prescribed means roughly this: he ordered this for this man as something suited to bring about health; and in the second it means that what happens to each man is in some way fixed for him to fit his destiny. This is what we mean when we say that things suit us, just as builders say of the squared stones in walls or pyramids that they suit one another, when they fit together in some connection. For there is altogether one fitness, one harmony. And just as the universe is made up out of all bodies to be the body it is, so out of all the existing causes destiny is made up to be the cause it is. Even people who understand nothing of this grasp my meaning, for they say, Fate brought this on him. So this was brought to him, this was prescribed for him. Let us then accept these things as we accept what Asclepius prescribes. Many of his prescriptions, too, are unpleasant, yet we accept them in hope of health. Let the carrying-out and completion of the things that the common nature judges good be regarded by you as on the same footing as your health. And so accept everything that happens, even if it seems unpleasant, because it leads to this: the health of the universe and the well-being and good fortune of Zeus, the universe itself. For he would not have brought on anyone what he has brought, if it were not useful for the whole. The nature of nothing whatever brings about anything unsuited to what it governs. So for two reasons you should be content with what happens to you: first, because it was done for you, prescribed for you, and in a way had reference to you, spun together with your destiny from the most ancient causes; and second, because even what comes to each man separately is, for the power that administers the universe, a cause of its well-being and completion, and indeed of its very continuance. For the integrity of the whole is maimed if you cut off anything at all from the connection and continuity of its parts or of its causes. And you do cut it off, as far as you can, when you are discontented, and in a way you try to do away with it.

Don't be disgusted, discouraged, or dissatisfied if you don't manage to do everything by sound principles. When you fail, go back and try again, and be content if most of what you do is consistent with human nature, and love the thing you return to. Don't go back to philosophy as if it were a stern master, but like a man with sore eyes who reaches for a bit of sponge and egg, or like another who applies a plaster, or a soak of water. That way you will not fail to obey reason, and you will find rest in it. Remember too that philosophy asks only for what your nature asks; it is you who want something else that is not according to nature. But, you may object, what is more agreeable than what I am doing now? Yet isn't this the very way pleasure deceives us? Consider whether greatness of soul, freedom, simplicity, calm, and devotion are not more agreeable still. And what is more agreeable than wisdom itself, when you think of the sureness and easy flow of everything that depends on the powers of understanding and knowledge?

Things are so wrapped up and obscure that they have seemed to philosophers, and not a few of them, nor commonplace ones, altogether unintelligible; indeed even to the Stoics themselves they seem hard to understand. And every judgment we make is liable to change, for where is the man who never changes his mind? Turn your thoughts, then, to the objects themselves, and consider how short-lived and worthless they are, and how they may be owned by a filthy wretch, a prostitute, or a thief. Then turn to the characters of those who live with you, and you can hardly bear even the most agreeable of them, let alone bear yourself. In such darkness and filth, then, and in such a ceaseless flow of substance and time, of motion and things moved, I cannot imagine what there is worth prizing highly or even pursuing seriously. On the contrary, a man's duty is to comfort himself and wait for his natural dissolution without fretting at the delay, resting only in these principles: first, that nothing will happen to me that is not in keeping with the nature of the universe; and second, that it is in my power never to act against my god and the guiding spirit within me, for no one can force me to do so.

What am I now using my soul for? On every occasion I must ask myself this, and examine what I now have in this part of me that they call the ruling principle, and whose soul I now have: a child's, a young man's, a weak woman's, a tyrant's, a tame animal's, or a wild beast's?

What sort of things the many consider good, we can learn even from this. If a man conceived of certain things as truly good, such as practical wisdom, self-control, justice, and courage, then having first grasped these he could not bear to hear anything that did not square with what is truly good. But if a man has first conceived as good the things the many call good, he will listen and gladly accept as very apt the line of the comic poet. In this way even the many sense the difference. For if it were otherwise, the saying would give offense and be rejected when applied to true goods, while we accept it as fitting and witty when it is said of wealth and of the means to luxury and fame. So go on and ask whether we should value, and judge to be good, the very things to which, once conceived in the mind, the comic poet's words could aptly be applied, that the man who has them has, through sheer abundance, nowhere even to relieve himself.

I am made up of the formal and the material; and neither of these will perish into nothing, just as neither came into being out of nothing. Every part of me, then, will be changed into some part of the universe, and that in turn into another part of the universe, and so on forever. By such a change I too came to exist, and so did those who begot me, and so on back forever in the other direction. For nothing stops us from saying this, even if the universe is administered in fixed cycles.

Reason and the art of reasoning, philosophy, are powers sufficient unto themselves and their own works. They set out from a starting point of their own and make their way to the goal set before them; and that is why such acts are called right acts, a word that signifies they proceed by the right road.

None of these things should be called a man's, which do not belong to a man as man. They are not required of a man, nor does man's nature promise them, nor are they the means by which his nature reaches its end. Therefore man's end does not lie in these things, nor does what helps toward that end, and what helps toward it is what is good. Besides, if any of these things did belong to man, it would not be right for him to despise them and set himself against them; nor would a man deserve praise for showing that he had no need of them, nor would a man who went without any of them be good, if these things really were good. But in fact, the more a man strips himself of these things, or others like them, or the more patiently he bears being deprived of any of them, by just so much is he the better man.

Such as are your habitual thoughts, such also will your mind's character be, for the soul is dyed by its thoughts. Dye it, then, with a continuous run of thoughts like these: that wherever a man can live, there he can also live well. But suppose he must live in a palace; well then, he can live well in a palace too. And consider further that whatever a thing has been made for, that is what it has been made for, and that is what it is carried toward; and its end lies in what it is carried toward; and where the end is, there too lie the advantage and the good of each thing. Now the good for a reasoning creature is society, for it has been shown above that we are made for society. Isn't it plain that the inferior exists for the sake of the superior? And living things are superior to lifeless ones, and among living things the superior are those that have reason.
To seek what is impossible is madness; and it is impossible for the bad not to do things of this kind.

Nothing happens to any man that he is not formed by nature to bear. The same things happen to another man, and either because he doesn't notice that they have happened, or because he wants to show greatness of spirit, he stands firm and remains unharmed. It is a disgrace, then, that ignorance and conceit should be stronger than wisdom.

Things in themselves do not touch the soul, not in the slightest; they have no access to the soul, and they cannot turn or move it. The soul alone turns and moves itself, and whatever judgments it sees fit to make, it makes for itself out of the things that present themselves to it.

In one respect a man is the thing nearest to me, in that I must do good to others and put up with them. But insofar as some men set themselves in the way of my proper actions, a man becomes to me one of the things that are indifferent, no less than the sun, the wind, or a wild beast. These may hinder my action, but they are no hindrance to my impulses and my disposition, which can act conditionally and adapt; for the mind turns and changes every obstacle to its activity into an aid, so that what was a hindrance becomes a help to action, and what blocks the road actually advances us along it.

Revere what is best in the universe, that which makes use of all things and directs all things. And in the same way revere what is best in yourself, for it is of the same kind. In you too, this is the thing that makes use of everything else, and by this your life is directed.

What does no harm to the state does no harm to the citizen. Whenever something appears harmful, apply this rule: if the state is not harmed by it, neither am I. But if the state is harmed, do not be angry with the one who harms it; instead, show him where his error lies.

Think often of how swiftly things pass by and vanish, both the things that exist and the things that are being produced. For substance is like a river in continual flow, the activities of things are forever changing, and the causes work in countless ways; there is hardly anything that stands still. And consider this thing close at hand, the boundless abyss of past and future, in which all things disappear. How then is the man not a fool who is puffed up over such things, or tormented by them, and makes himself miserable? For they trouble him only for a time, and a short time at that.

Think of the universal substance, of which you are a very small part; and of universal time, of which a brief, indivisible moment has been allotted to you; and of destiny, of which you are how tiny a portion.

Does another do me wrong? Let him see to it. He has his own disposition and his own way of acting. For my part, I now have what the universal nature now wills me to have, and I do what my own nature now wills me to do.

Let the part of your soul that leads and governs stay undisturbed by the movements of the flesh, whether of pleasure or of pain. Let it not mingle with them, but keep itself separate and confine those feelings to their own parts of the body. But when these feelings rise up to the mind through the natural sympathy that exists in a body that is all one, then do not try to resist the sensation, for it is natural; only do not let the ruling part add to the sensation the opinion that it is either good or bad.

Live with the gods. And he lives with the gods who constantly shows them that his soul is satisfied with what is assigned to him, and that it does all that the guiding spirit wishes, the spirit that Zeus has given to each man as his guardian and guide, a portion of himself. And this is each man's understanding and reason.

Are you angry with the man whose armpits stink? Are you angry with the man whose breath smells foul? What good will your anger do you? He has such a mouth, he has such armpits; from such things such an odor must come. But the man has reason, you say, and could, if he took the trouble, work out where he is offending. Good luck to you with that discovery. Well then, you too have reason: use your rational faculty to rouse his; show him his error, set him straight. If he listens, you will cure him, and there is no need of anger. Neither tragic actor nor prostitute.

As you intend to live once you have departed, so it is in your power to live here. But if men will not allow it, then leave life, yet as one who suffers no harm by it. The room is smoky, and I walk out. Why think this any great trouble? But so long as nothing of the kind drives me out, I stay, I am free, and no one shall stop me from doing what I choose; and I choose to act according to the nature of a rational and social creature.

The intelligence of the universe is social. Accordingly it has made the inferior things for the sake of the superior, and it has fitted the superior to one another. You see how it has subordinated and coordinated them, assigning to each its proper portion, and bringing the best things into harmony with one another.

How have you behaved up to now toward the gods, toward your parents, brothers, children, teachers, toward those who cared for you in infancy, toward your friends, your relatives, your slaves? Consider whether up to now you have behaved toward them all in such a way that this could be said of you:
Never has he wronged a man in deed or word.

And call to mind how many things you have lived through, and how much you have been able to endure; that the story of your life is now complete and your service ended; how many beautiful things you have seen; how many pleasures and pains you have looked past; how many so-called honors you have spurned; and to how many ill-natured people you have shown a kind disposition.

Why do unskilled and ignorant souls disturb the one who has skill and knowledge? And what soul has skill and knowledge? The one that knows the beginning and the end, and knows the reason that runs through all substance and, throughout all time, administers the universe in fixed cycles.

Soon, very soon, you will be ashes or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and a name is mere sound and echo. The things much prized in life are empty and rotten and trivial, like little dogs snapping at one another, or little children quarreling, laughing, and the next moment in tears.
