But loyalty and modesty and justice and truth have fled away,
up to Olympus from the wide-spread earth.

What, then, is left to keep you here, if the objects of sense are forever shifting and never stand still, if the organs of perception are dull and easily take in false impressions, and the poor soul itself is but a vapor risen from blood? To have a good reputation in such a world as this is an empty thing. Why then do you not wait calmly for your end, whether it be extinction or a passing into another state? And until that time comes, what is enough? Why, what else than to honor the gods and bless them, to do good to others, to practice tolerance and self-restraint; and as for everything beyond the bounds of this poor flesh and breath, to remember that it is neither yours nor in your power.

You can spend your life in an even flow of happiness, if you can go by the right road and think and act in the right way. These two things are common to the soul of God, to the soul of man, and to the soul of every rational being: not to be hindered by another, and to find the good in a disposition toward justice and the practice of it, and there to let your desire come to rest.
If this is not my own badness, nor the effect of my own badness, and the common good is not harmed by it, why am I troubled about it, and what is the harm to the common good?

Do not be carried away thoughtlessly by the appearance of things, but give help to all according to your ability and their need; and if they have suffered loss in matters that are indifferent, do not imagine this to be real damage, for that is a bad habit. But just as the old man, when he was leaving, asked back his foster-child's top, remembering all the while that it was only a top, so do you act in this case too.

When you are out there declaiming on the public platform, have you forgotten, man, what these things really are? Yes, but they matter greatly to these people. Will you then let yourself be made a fool of along with them? I was once a fortunate man, but I lost it, I don't know how. But fortunate means a man who has assigned himself a good lot, and a good lot is a good disposition of the soul, good impulses, good actions.

The substance of the universe is obedient and yielding, and the reason that governs it has in itself no cause to do evil, for it holds no malice, does evil to nothing, and harms nothing. All things are made and brought to completion according to this reason.

Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm, as long as you are doing your duty; whether you are drowsy or fully rested; whether spoken ill of or praised; whether dying or doing something else. For dying is one of the acts of life, and in this act too it is enough to do well what we have in hand.
Look within. Do not let the particular quality of anything, or its worth, escape you.
All existing things change soon, and they will either be reduced to vapor, if indeed all substance is one, or else they will be scattered.
The reason that governs knows its own disposition, what it does, and the material on which it works.
The best way to avenge yourself is not to become like the wrongdoer.
Take pleasure and rest in one thing: in passing from one act done for others to another act done for others, with God in your thoughts.
The ruling part of you is what rouses and turns itself; it makes itself such as it is and such as it wills to be, and it also makes everything that happens appear to itself as it wills.

Every single thing is brought to completion in accordance with the nature of the universe; for it cannot be in accordance with any other nature that each thing is accomplished, neither a nature that contains this one from outside, nor a nature contained within it, nor a nature external to it and independent.

The universe is either confusion, things tangled together and scattered apart, or else it is unity, order, and providence. If it is the former, why do I wish to linger in a random jumble of things, in such disorder? Why should I care about anything except how I shall at last become earth? And why am I disturbed, since my elements will be scattered whatever I do? But if the other view is true, then I revere, I stand firm, and I trust in the one who governs.

When circumstances have forced you into some disturbance, return quickly to yourself, and do not stay out of tune any longer than the compulsion lasts; for you will gain greater mastery over the harmony by continually coming back to it.

If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would do your duty by the stepmother, yet you would constantly return to your mother. Let the court and philosophy now be your stepmother and your mother: return to philosophy often and find rest in her, for through her what you meet with at court becomes bearable to you, and you become bearable at court.

When we have meat and such food before us, we get the impression: this is the dead body of a fish, this the dead body of a bird or a pig; and again, this fine Falernian wine is only a little grape juice, this purple robe just sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shellfish. Such impressions reach the things themselves and penetrate them, so that we see what kind of things they really are. We should act this way all through life: where things seem most worthy of our approval, lay them bare, look at how worthless they are, and strip away the words that exalt them. For outward show is a wonderful corrupter of reason, and it cheats you most when you are most sure you are busy with things worth your trouble. Consider, then, what Crates says of Xenocrates himself.

Most of the things the crowd admires belong to the most general categories, things held together by mere cohesion or natural growth, such as stones, wood, fig trees, vines, olives. The things admired by men a little more reasonable are held together by a living principle, like flocks and herds. The things admired by men still better instructed are held together by a rational soul, though not a universal one, only a soul skilled in some craft or expert in some other way, or simply rational in the sense of owning a number of slaves. But the man who values a rational soul, one that is universal and fitted for life in society, regards nothing else; above all he keeps his own soul in a state and activity in keeping with reason and social life, and he works toward this end together with others of his own kind.

Some things are hurrying into existence, others hurrying out of it; and of what is coming into being, part is already gone. Motions and changes are continually renewing the world, just as the unbroken passage of time is always renewing the infinite stretch of ages. In this flowing stream, where there is no firm footing, what is there among the things rushing by that anyone should prize highly? It would be like falling in love with one of the sparrows flying past, when it has already passed out of sight. Something like this is the very life of each of us, like the rising of vapor from the blood and the breathing of air. For just as it is to draw in the air once and give it back, which we do every moment, so it is with the whole power of breathing that you received at your birth, only yesterday or the day before, and give back to the element from which you first drew it.

Transpiration, as in plants, is nothing to be valued; nor is breathing, as in tame animals and wild beasts; nor receiving impressions through the appearances of things; nor being pulled about by desires like a puppet by strings; nor herding together; nor being nourished by food, which is just like getting rid of the useless part of what we eat. What, then, is worth valuing? To be applauded? No. Nor should we value the applause of tongues, for the praise of the many is just a clapping of tongues. So suppose you have given up this worthless thing called fame; what remains worth valuing? This, in my opinion: to move yourself and to hold yourself back in keeping with your own constitution, the end to which all employments and arts lead. For every art aims at this, that the thing made should be fit for the work it was made for; and the vine grower tending his vine, the horse breaker, and the dog trainer all seek this end. And the education and teaching of the young aim at something too. Here, then, lies the value of education and teaching. And if this is sound, you will not seek anything else. Will you not stop valuing so many other things? Then you will be neither free, nor self-sufficient for your own happiness, nor free from passion. For you must of necessity be envious, jealous, and suspicious of those who can take those things away, and you will plot against those who have what you value. Anyone who wants any of these things must necessarily be in a state of inner turmoil, and besides, he must often find fault with the gods. But to reverence and honor your own mind will make you content with yourself, in harmony with society, and in agreement with the gods, that is, praising all that they give and have ordained.

Above, below, all around are the movements of the elements. But the motion of virtue is in none of these: it is something more divine, and advancing by a path scarcely noticed, it goes happily on its way.

How strangely people act! They will not praise those living at the same time and alongside them; yet to be praised themselves by future generations, by people they have never seen and never will see, they set great store. But this is much the same as being grieved that those who lived before you did not praise you.

If something is hard for you to accomplish, do not conclude that it is impossible for any human being; but if anything is possible for a human being and in keeping with his nature, consider that it is within your reach too.

Suppose in the wrestling ground a man has scratched you with his nails or struck your head and given you a bruise. We show no sign of being upset, take no offense, and do not afterward suspect him of foul play; yet we keep an eye on him, not as an enemy, nor with suspicion, but we quietly steer clear of him. Let your conduct be like this in all the other parts of life: let us overlook many things in those who are like our opponents in the ring. For it is in our power, as I said, to get out of the way and to hold no suspicion or hatred.

If anyone can convince me and show me that I am not thinking or acting rightly, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no one was ever harmed. But the one who is harmed is the one who persists in his own error and ignorance.
I do my duty: other things do not trouble me, for they are either things without life, or things without reason, or things that have wandered off and lost their way.

As for the animals that have no reason, and indeed all things and objects, since you have reason and they do not, make use of them in a generous and openhanded spirit. But toward human beings, since they have reason, behave in a spirit of fellowship. And on every occasion call on the gods; and do not worry about how long you will go on doing this, for even three hours so spent are enough.

Alexander of Macedon and his stable boy were brought by death to the same state; for either they were taken up into the same generative principles of the universe, or they were alike scattered among the atoms.

Consider how many things take place in each of us in a single indivisible moment, things concerning the body and things concerning the soul; then you will not be surprised that far more, indeed all things that come into being, exist at the same time in that single whole which we call the Cosmos.

If someone put to you the question of how the name Antoninus is spelled, would you strain your voice as you uttered each letter? And if they grew angry, would you grow angry too? Would you not calmly go on and count out every letter? Just so in this life, remember that every duty is made up of certain parts. It is your duty to observe these, and without being disturbed or showing anger toward those who are angry with you, to go on your way and finish what is set before you.

How cruel it is not to let people pursue the things that seem to them suited to their nature and to their advantage! And yet, in a way, you do not allow them this when you are vexed because they do wrong. For they are surely drawn toward such things because they suppose them suited to their nature and to their advantage. But it is not so. Then teach them, and show them, without being angry.
Death is a cessation of impressions through the senses, of the tugging of the strings that move our appetites, of the ranging movements of our thoughts, and of our service to the flesh.
It is a shame for the soul to give way first in this life, while your body does not give way.

Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not stained with that dye; for such things happen. Keep yourself simple, good, pure, serious, free of pretense, a friend of justice, a worshiper of the gods, kind, affectionate, and vigorous in all proper acts. Strive to remain such as philosophy wished to make you. Reverence the gods and help your fellow human beings. Life is short. The one fruit of this earthly life is a devout disposition and acts done for others. Do everything as a disciple of Antoninus. Remember his steadiness in every act done in keeping with reason, his evenness in all things, his piety, the serenity of his face, his sweetness, his disregard for empty fame, and his efforts to understand things; how he would never let anything pass without first examining it most carefully and understanding it clearly; how he bore with those who blamed him unjustly without blaming them back; how he did nothing in a hurry; how he refused to listen to slanders; how careful an examiner he was of characters and actions; how he was not given to reproaching people, nor timid, nor suspicious, nor a hairsplitter; how little contented him in lodging, bed, dress, food, and servants; how hardworking and patient he was; how, thanks to his sparing diet, he could hold out till evening, not even needing to relieve himself except at the usual hour; his firmness and constancy in his friendships; how he tolerated frank opposition to his opinions; the pleasure he took when anyone showed him something better; and how religious he was, without superstition. Imitate all this, so that when your last hour comes you may have as good a conscience as he had.

Return to your sober senses and call yourself back; and when you have roused yourself from sleep and realized that it was only dreams that troubled you, then, awake again, look at the things around you as you looked at those dreams.

I am made up of a little body and a soul. To this little body all things are indifferent, for it cannot perceive differences. But to the understanding, only those things are indifferent that are not the work of its own activity; whatever is the work of its own activity is all within its power. And even of these, only those done with reference to the present, for as to the mind's future and past activities, even these are for the present indifferent.

Neither the labor done by the hand nor that done by the foot is contrary to nature, so long as the foot does the foot's work and the hand the hand's. So too a man's labor is not contrary to nature, as long as it does the things proper to a man. And if the labor is not contrary to his nature, neither is it an evil to him.
How many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, murderers of their own fathers, and tyrants.

Do you not see how craftsmen accommodate themselves up to a point to those unskilled in their trade, and yet hold fast to the principles of their art and will not bear to depart from them? Is it not strange, then, that the architect and the physician should have more respect for the principles of their own arts than a man has for his own reason, which he shares with the gods?

Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the whole sea is a drop in the universe; Mount Athos a little clod of it; all present time a single point in eternity. All things are small, changeable, and perishable. All things come from that one universal ruling power, either directly or as a consequence. And so the lion's gaping jaws, and poison, and every harmful thing, like a thorn or like mud, are by-products of what is grand and beautiful. Do not imagine, then, that they are of a different kind from what you revere, but form a just opinion of the source of all things.
Whoever has seen present things has seen everything, both all that has happened from eternity and all that will be through endless time; for all things are of one kind and one form.

Frequently consider how all things in the universe are connected and related to one another. For in a way all things are interwoven, and so all are friendly to one another; for one thing follows another in order, and this is by virtue of their active movement, their working together, and the unity of the substance.
Adapt yourself to the things your lot has cast you among; and the people among whom your portion has fallen, love them, but truly and sincerely.

Every instrument, tool, or vessel does well if it does what it was made for, and yet the one who made it is not present in it. But in things held together by nature, the power that made them is within and abides in them; and for this reason it is all the more fitting to reverence that power, and to consider that if you live and act according to its will, everything in you is in keeping with intelligence. And so too in the universe, the things that belong to it are in keeping with intelligence.

Whatever of the things not in your power you suppose to be good or evil for you, then necessarily, if such an evil befalls you or you lose such a good, you will blame the gods and hate other people too, those who caused the misfortune or the loss, or those suspected of being likely to cause it; and indeed we do much wrong because we draw a distinction over these things. But if we judge only what is in our power to be good or bad, no reason remains either for finding fault with God or for taking a hostile stance toward any human being.

We are all working together toward one end, some knowingly and by design, others without knowing what they do, just as people do even while asleep, of whom it is Heraclitus, I think, who says that they too are workers and fellow contributors to what happens in the universe. But people cooperate in different ways: even those cooperate abundantly who find fault with what happens and try to oppose and hinder it, for the universe had need even of such men. It remains, then, for you to understand which kind of worker you place yourself among; for the one who governs all things will certainly make right use of you, and will receive you among some group of cooperators whose labors lead to one end. Only do not be such a part as the mean and ridiculous line in the play that Chrysippus speaks of.

Does the sun take on the work of the rain, or Asclepius the work of the earth that bears fruit? And what of each of the stars: are they not different, and yet do they not work together toward the same end?

If the gods have made decisions about me and about the things that must happen to me, they have decided well, for it is not easy even to imagine a deity without foresight; and as for harming me, why would they have any wish to do so? What advantage would come to them from this, or to the whole, which is the special object of their providence? But if they have made no decision about me individually, they have certainly decided about the whole at least, and the things that happen as a consequence of this general arrangement I ought to accept gladly and be content with. But if they decide about nothing, which it is wicked to believe, and if we do believe it, then let us neither sacrifice, nor pray, nor swear by them, nor do anything else we do as though the gods were present and lived among us; but even if the gods decide about none of the things that concern us, I am able to decide about myself, and I can inquire into what is useful; and what is useful to each person is what is in keeping with his own constitution and nature. Now my nature is rational and social; and my city and country, insofar as I am Antoninus, is Rome, but insofar as I am a man, it is the world. The things that are useful to these cities, then, are the only things useful to me.

Whatever happens to anyone is for the good of the whole: this alone might be enough. But further you will observe this as a general truth, if you observe carefully, that whatever is profitable to one person is profitable to others too. But let the word profitable be taken here in the ordinary sense, as said of things of the middle kind, neither good nor bad.

Just as in the amphitheater and such places the constant sight of the same things and their sameness make the show tiresome, so it is with the whole of life; for all things, above and below, are the same and come from the same source. How long, then?

Think continually that all kinds of people, all kinds of pursuits, all sorts of nations are dead, so that your thoughts go right down even to Philistion, Phoebus, and Origanion. Now turn your thoughts to the other kinds of men. To that place we too must move, where there are so many great orators, so many noble philosophers, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates; so many heroes of former days, and so many generals after them, and tyrants; and besides these, Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, and other men of sharp natural talent, great minds, lovers of work, versatile, bold, even mockers of the perishable and fleeting life of man, like Menippus and those like him. Consider that all of these have long been in the dust. What harm is this to them, then; and what to those whose names are utterly unknown? One thing here is worth a great deal: to pass your life in truth and justice, with goodwill even toward liars and unjust men.

When you wish to give yourself joy, think of the virtues of those who live with you, for instance the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth. For nothing gives such joy as the examples of the virtues, when they are displayed in the characters of those who live with us and present themselves to us as fully as possible. So we should keep them before our eyes.

You are not dissatisfied, I suppose, because you weigh only so many pounds and not three hundred. Then do not be dissatisfied that you must live only so many years and not more; for just as you are content with the amount of matter assigned to you, so be content with the amount of time.

Let us try to persuade people. But act even against their will when the principles of justice point that way. If, however, anyone uses force to stand in your way, turn to contentment and tranquillity, and at the same time use the obstacle to exercise some other virtue; and remember that your attempt was made with a reservation, that you did not desire to do the impossible. What, then, did you desire? Just such an effort as this. And in that you succeed, even if the things you were aiming at are not accomplished.
The one who loves fame thinks another man's activity is his own good; the one who loves pleasure thinks his own sensations are; but the one who has understanding thinks his own acts are his own good.
It is in our power to hold no opinion about a thing and not to be disturbed in our soul; for things in themselves have no natural power to shape our judgments.
Train yourself to attend carefully to what another person says, and as far as possible to enter into the speaker's mind.
What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee either.

If sailors abused the helmsman, or the sick abused the doctor, would they then listen to anyone else? Or how could the helmsman secure the safety of those in the ship, or the doctor the health of those he attends?
How many of those with whom I came into the world have already gone out of it.

To the jaundiced, honey tastes bitter; to those bitten by mad dogs, water brings terror; and to little children, a ball seems a fine thing. Why, then, am I angry? Do you think a false opinion has less power than the bile in the jaundiced man or the poison in the one bitten by a mad dog?
No one will keep you from living according to the reason of your own nature; nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of universal nature.
What sort of people are those whom men wish to please, and for what ends, and by what kind of acts? How soon will time cover all things, and how many it has covered already.

What is wickedness? It is something you have seen many times before. With everything that happens, keep this in mind: it is something you have seen many times before. Up and down, everywhere, you will find the same things, the things that fill the old histories, the histories of past ages and of our own day, the things that fill cities and households now. There is nothing new. All of it is both familiar and short-lived.

How can your principles die, unless the thoughts that match them are snuffed out? But it is in your power to keep fanning these thoughts back into flame. I am able to hold whatever opinion I ought to hold about anything. If I am able, why am I troubled? The things outside my mind have no bearing on my mind at all. Once your feelings reach this state, you stand upright. To recover your life is in your power. Look at things again the way you used to look at them, for in this lies the recovery of your life.

The pointless business of pageantry, plays on the stage, flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, sparring with spears, a bone tossed to puppies, a crumb of bread dropped into fishponds, the toil and load-hauling of ants, the scurrying of frightened little mice, puppets jerked on strings, all of it the same. It is your duty, then, in the midst of such things, to be good-humored and not put on airs, while understanding that every person is worth exactly as much as the things he busies himself with.

In conversation you must pay attention to what is being said, and in every action you must watch what is being done. In the one, look at once to the end it is aiming at; in the other, watch carefully for what is really meant.

Is my mind equal to this task or not? If it is equal to it, I use it for the work as an instrument given me by universal nature. But if it is not equal to it, then either I step back from the work and yield to someone better able to do it, unless there is some reason I ought not, or I do it as well as I can, calling in to help me the person who, with the guidance of my ruling mind, can do what is now fitting and useful for the common good. For whatever I do, whether by myself or with another, ought to be aimed at this alone: at what is useful and well suited to society.
How many who were celebrated by fame have been handed over to oblivion, and how many who celebrated the fame of others have themselves long been dead.

Do not be ashamed to be helped, for it is your business to do your duty like a soldier storming a town. So what if, being lame, you cannot scale the battlements alone, but with another's help it can be done?
Do not let things to come trouble you, for you will meet them, if you must, carrying with you the same reason you now use for the things at hand.

All things are bound up with one another, and the bond is sacred; hardly anything is unconnected to anything else. For things have been arranged together, and they combine to make up one and the same universe. There is one universe made of all things, and one God who pervades all things, and one substance, and one law, one common reason in all intelligent creatures, and one truth, if indeed there is also one perfection for all creatures that share the same origin and partake of reason.

Everything material soon vanishes back into the substance of the whole; everything that gives form is very soon taken back into the universal reason; and the memory of everything is very soon swallowed up in time.
For the rational creature, the same act is both according to nature and according to reason.
Stand upright, or be set upright.

Just as it is with the parts of a single united body, so it is with rational beings, which exist separately yet have been made for one shared work. The awareness of this will become clearer to you if you often say to yourself: I am a limb of the body of rational beings. But if you say you are merely a part, you do not yet love your fellow human beings from the heart; doing good does not yet delight you for its own sake; you still do it merely as something proper, and not yet as doing good to yourself.

Let whatever will fall from outside fall upon the parts that can feel its impact. Those parts that have felt it may complain, if they choose. But I, unless I judge what has happened to be an evil, am not harmed. And it is in my power not to judge it so.
Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good, just as if the gold, or the emerald, or the purple were forever saying: whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and keep my color.

The ruling faculty does not disturb itself; I mean, it does not frighten itself or cause itself pain. But if anyone else can frighten or pain it, let him try. For the faculty itself will not, by its own opinion, turn itself toward such states. Let the body itself take care, if it can, that it suffers nothing, and let it speak up if it does suffer. But the soul itself, the part that is subject to fear and pain and has full power to form an opinion about these things, will suffer nothing, for it will never slide into such a judgment. The ruling principle in itself wants nothing, unless it creates a want for itself; and so it is free from disturbance and unobstructed, as long as it does not disturb and obstruct itself.

Happiness is a good spirit, or a good thing. So what are you doing here, imagination? Go away, I beg you by the gods, the same way you came, for I have no need of you. But you have come in your old habitual way. I am not angry with you; only go away.

Is anyone afraid of change? Why, what can happen at all without change? What is more pleasing or more natural to universal nature? Can you take a bath unless the wood undergoes change? Can you be nourished unless the food undergoes change? Can anything useful at all be accomplished without change? Do you not see, then, that for you to change is just the same thing, and equally necessary to universal nature?

Through the universal substance, as through a raging torrent, all bodies are swept along, united with the whole by their nature and working together with it, like the parts of our body with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has time already swallowed up! And let the same thought come to you about every person and every thing.
Only one thing troubles me: that I might do something the constitution of man does not allow, or in a way it does not allow, or that it does not allow now.
Near is your forgetting of all things, and near is your being forgotten by all.

It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong. This happens when it occurs to you, as they do wrong, that they are your kin, that they do wrong through ignorance and without meaning to, that soon you will both be dead, and above all that the wrongdoer has done you no harm, for he has not made your ruling faculty any worse than it was before.

Universal nature, out of the universal substance as if it were wax, now molds a horse, and when it has broken that up, uses the material for a tree, then for a man, then for something else; and each of these lasts only a very short time. But it is no hardship for the vessel to be broken up, just as there was none in its being put together.

A scowling look is entirely unnatural; when it is often put on, the result is that all comeliness dies away, and at last is so completely extinguished that it cannot be rekindled at all. Try to draw from this very fact the conclusion that it is contrary to reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong should leave you, what reason is there to go on living?

The nature that governs the whole will soon change everything you see, and out of their substance will make other things, and again other things out of the substance of those, so that the world may be forever new.

When someone has wronged you, consider at once what notion of good or evil led him to do wrong. For once you have seen this, you will pity him, and you will neither be amazed nor angry. For either you yourself hold the same thing to be good that he does, or something else of the same kind, in which case it is your duty to forgive him. But if you do not regard such things as good or evil, you will all the more readily be kindly toward someone who is in error.

Think not so much of what you do not have as of what you do have, and of the things you have, pick out the best, and then reflect how eagerly you would have hunted for them if you did not have them. At the same time, take care that you do not, by being so pleased with them, get into the habit of overvaluing them, so that you would be upset if you ever lost them.
Withdraw into yourself. The rational principle that rules has this nature: it is content with itself when it does what is just, and so secures its own tranquility.

Wipe out the imagination. Stop the pulling of the strings. Confine yourself to the present. Understand well what is happening, whether to you or to another. Divide and break down every object into its cause and its matter. Think of your last hour. Let the wrong done by another stay there, where the wrong was done.
Direct your attention to what is being said. Let your understanding enter into the things being done and into the things doing them.

Adorn yourself with simplicity and modesty, and with indifference toward the things that lie between virtue and vice. Love humankind. Follow God. The poet says that law rules all, and it is enough to remember that law rules all.
About death: whether it is a scattering, or a dissolution into atoms, or annihilation, it is either an extinguishing or a change.

About pain: pain that is unbearable carries us off, but pain that lasts a long time is bearable; and the mind keeps its own tranquility by withdrawing into itself, and the ruling faculty is not made any worse. As for the parts that are harmed by pain, let them, if they can, speak their opinion about it.

About fame: look at the minds of those who chase it, observe what they are, and what sort of things they avoid, and what sort of things they pursue. And consider that, just as heaps of sand piled on one another bury the earlier sand, so in life the events that come before are soon buried by those that come after.

From Plato: Do you suppose it possible for a man with an elevated mind, who takes in the whole of time and the whole of substance, to think human life is anything great? It is not possible, he said. Then such a man will think that death too is no evil. Certainly not.
From Antisthenes: It is kingly to do good and to be abused for it.
It is a disgraceful thing for the face to be obedient, arranging and composing itself as the mind commands, while the mind does not arrange and compose itself.
It is no use being angry at events, for they care nothing about it.
To the immortal gods and to us give joy.
Life must be reaped like ripe ears of grain. One man is born; another dies.
Earth must be given back to earth; then life, for all, must be reaped like the harvest, as necessity commands.
If the gods care nothing for me and my children, there is a reason for it.
For the good is with me, and the just.
No joining others in their wailing, no violent passion.

From Plato: But I would give this man a sufficient answer, which is this. You speak wrongly if you think that a man worth anything at all ought to weigh the risk of life or death, and not rather look to this one thing in everything he does: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, the work of a good man or of a bad one.

For the truth is this, men of Athens: wherever a man has stationed himself, thinking it the best place for him, or has been stationed by his commander, there, in my opinion, he ought to stay and face the danger, reckoning nothing, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace.

But, my good friend, consider whether what is noble and good is not something other than saving your life and being saved. As for a man's living a certain length of time, at least if he is truly a man, consider whether this is not something to be put out of mind; there must be no clinging to life. A man must entrust these matters to the Deity and believe what the women say, that no one can escape his destiny, and the next question is how he may best live the time he has to live.

Look around at the courses of the stars, as if you were traveling along with them, and constantly consider how the elements change into one another, for such thoughts wash away the grime of life on earth.

This is a fine saying of Plato's: that whoever is discussing human beings should also look at earthly things as if viewing them from some higher place, looking at them in their gatherings, armies, farm labor, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, the uproar of the law courts, lonely places, the various tribes of barbarians, festivals, mournings, marketplaces, a mixture of all things and an orderly weaving together of opposites.

Consider the past, all those great shifts of political power; you can foresee the things to come as well. For they will certainly take the same form, and they cannot possibly stray from the pattern of what happens now. And so to have observed human life for forty years is the same as to have observed it for ten thousand. For what more will you see?
What has grown from the earth returns to the earth; but what has sprung from heavenly seed returns to the realms of heaven.
This is either a breaking apart of the atoms woven together, or a like scattering of the senseless elements.
With food and drink and cunning magic arts, turning the channel's course to escape death. The breeze that heaven has sent we must endure, and toil without complaint.
Another may be more skilled at throwing his opponent, but he is no more sociable, no more modest, no better trained to meet whatever happens, no more considerate of his neighbors' faults.

Wherever a work can be done in keeping with the reason common to gods and men, there we have nothing to fear; for where we can gain benefit through activity that succeeds and proceeds according to our constitution, there no harm is to be suspected.

Everywhere and always it is in your power to accept your present condition with reverence, to behave justly toward those around you, and to apply your skill to your present thoughts, so that nothing slips into them without being well examined.

Do not look around you to discover other people's ruling principles, but look straight to this: to what nature is leading you, both universal nature through the things that happen to you, and your own nature through the acts you must perform. Every being ought to do what accords with its constitution. All other things have been made for the sake of rational beings, just as among irrational things the lower exists for the sake of the higher; but rational beings exist for the sake of one another.

The chief principle, then, in man's constitution is the social one. The second is not to give in to the urgings of the body, for it is the special office of the rational and intelligent motion to set its own limits and never to be overpowered by the motion of the senses or of the appetites, since both of these are animal; the intelligent motion claims supremacy and does not allow itself to be overpowered by the others. And rightly so, for it is formed by nature to make use of them all. The third thing in the rational constitution is freedom from error and from deception. Let the ruling principle, then, hold fast to these and go straight on, and it has what is its own.
Consider yourself dead, and that you have completed your life up to the present; and live the rest that is allowed you according to nature.
Love only what happens to you and is spun for you by the thread of your destiny. For what could suit you better?

In everything that happens, keep before your eyes those to whom the same things happened, and how they were vexed, and treated them as strange, and found fault with them. And now, where are they? Nowhere. Why, then, do you choose to act the same way? Why not leave these agitations, which are foreign to nature, to those who stir them up and those who are stirred by them? Why not be wholly intent on the right use of the things that happen to you? For then you will use them well, and they will be material for you to work on. Only attend to yourself, and resolve to be a good man in everything you do; and remember...
Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will keep bubbling up, if you will keep digging.

The body ought to be steady and to show no awkwardness in motion or posture. For what the mind shows in the face by keeping there an expression of intelligence and good order, that should be asked of the whole body as well. But all of this should be done without affectation.
The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing, in that it should stand ready and firm to meet whatever comes at it, sudden and unexpected.

Constantly observe who the people are whose approval you want, and what ruling principles they have. For then you will neither blame those who offend without meaning to, nor crave their approval, once you look to the sources of their opinions and desires.

Every soul, the philosopher says, is robbed of the truth against its will; and in the same way it is robbed of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of the sort. It is most necessary to keep this constantly in mind, for then you will be gentler toward everyone.

In every pain, let this thought be present: that there is no dishonor in it, and that it does not make the governing intelligence any worse, for it does no damage to the intelligence either as rational or as social. In most pains, too, let this remark of Epicurus help you: that pain is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you keep in mind that it has its limits and add nothing to it in your imagination. And remember this as well, that many things which annoy us are really the same as pain, though we do not notice it, such as drowsiness, being scorched by heat, and having no appetite. So whenever you are discontented over any of these, say to yourself that you are giving in to pain.
Take care not to feel toward the inhuman the way they feel toward other people.

How do we know that Telauges was not finer in character than Socrates? It is not enough that Socrates died a more noble death, argued more skillfully with the sophists, endured a night in the cold with greater toughness, and that, when ordered to arrest Leon of Salamis, judged it nobler to refuse, and that he walked the streets with a swagger, though one may well doubt whether that last point is even true. What we ought to ask is what sort of soul Socrates had, and whether he was able to be content with being just toward men and reverent toward the gods, neither pointlessly vexed at men's villainy, nor making himself a slave to any man's ignorance, nor treating anything that fell to his lot from the universe as strange, nor enduring it as unbearable, nor letting his understanding share in the feelings of the poor flesh.

Nature has not so blended the intelligence with the body's makeup as to deny you the power of setting your own limits and bringing under your control all that is your own; for it is quite possible to be a godlike man and to be recognized as such by no one. Always bear this in mind, and this too: that very little indeed is needed to live a happy life. And just because you have given up hope of becoming a logician and an expert in the knowledge of nature, do not for that reason give up the hope of being free and modest and social and obedient to God.

It is in your power to live free from all compulsion, in the greatest tranquility of mind, even if the whole world shouts against you all it likes, even if wild beasts tear apart the limbs of this lump of matter that has grown up around you. For what prevents the mind, in the midst of all this, from keeping itself in tranquility, in a just judgment of all that surrounds it, and in a ready use of whatever is set before it? So that the judgment may say to the thing it observes: This is what you are in reality, though in men's opinion you may seem to be something else. And the use may say to whatever comes to hand: You are the thing I was looking for; for to me whatever presents itself is always material for virtue, both rational and civic, and, in a word, for the practice of an art that belongs to man or God. For everything that happens is related either to God or to man, and is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and fit material to work on.
The perfection of character lies in this: in passing every day as if it were your last, neither violently agitated nor sluggish nor playing the hypocrite.

The gods, who are immortal, are not annoyed that for so long a time they must put up with men as they are, and so many of them bad; and besides this, they even take care of them in every way. But you, who are bound to die so soon, are you tired of putting up with the bad, and this when you are one of them?
It is absurd for a man not to flee from his own badness, which is in fact possible, but to flee from other men's badness, which is impossible.
Whatever the rational and social faculty finds to be neither intelligent nor social, it rightly judges to be beneath itself.

When you have done a good deed and another has been the better for it, why do you still go looking for some third thing besides, as fools do, either to get the reputation of having done a good deed or to be repaid?
No one tires of receiving what is useful. But acting according to nature is useful. So do not tire of receiving what is useful by doing it for others.

The nature of the All set itself in motion to make the universe. Now, either everything that happens follows by way of consequence and connection, or else even the chief things toward which the ruling power of the universe directs its own movement are governed by no rational principle. If you remember this, it will make you more tranquil in many situations.

This reflection also helps remove the craving for empty fame: it is no longer in your power to have lived your whole life, or even your life from youth onward, as a philosopher. It is plain, both to many others and to yourself, that you are far from being a philosopher. You have fallen into a confused way of living, so it is no longer easy for you to gain the reputation of a philosopher, and your manner of life works against it too. So if you have truly seen how matters stand, let go of the question of how you will appear to others, and be content to live the rest of your life as your nature wills. Notice, then, what it wills, and let nothing else distract you. You have wandered far and wide and found happiness nowhere: not in logical arguments, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in pleasure, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature requires. And how does a person do this? By holding to principles from which their feelings and actions flow. What principles? Those about good and bad: the belief that nothing is good for a person unless it makes them just, self-controlled, courageous, and free, and that nothing is bad unless it produces the opposite of these.

With every action you take, ask yourself: How does this affect me? Will I regret it? In a little while I will be dead and all of this will be gone. What more do I want, as long as what I am doing now is the work of an intelligent being, a social being, one who lives under the same law as God?

Alexander, Caesar, and Pompey, what are they compared to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? Those philosophers understood the realities of things, their causes, their substance, and their guiding principles were aligned with their pursuits. But as for the others, how many things they had to worry about, and to how many things they were enslaved!
Bear in mind that people will go on doing the same things regardless, even if you burst with frustration.

This is the main thing: do not be disturbed, for all things happen according to the nature of the universe, and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just like Hadrian and Augustus. Next, fix your eyes steadily on the task before you, look at it, and at the same time remember that it is your duty to be a good person and to do what human nature demands, doing it without wavering; and say what seems to you most just, but say it with good will, with modesty, and without pretense.

The nature of the universe has this work to do: to move the things that are here to elsewhere, to change them, to take them away from here, and to carry them there. All things are change, yet we have no reason to fear anything new. All things are familiar to us, and their distribution always stays the same.

Every nature is content with itself when it follows its proper course, and a rational nature follows its proper course when it gives its assent to nothing false or uncertain in its thoughts, when it directs its impulses only toward social action, when it limits its desires and aversions to things within its power, and when it is satisfied with everything assigned to it by the universal nature. For of this universal nature every particular nature is a part, just as the nature of a leaf is part of the nature of a plant; except that the leaf's nature is part of a nature that has no perception or reason and can be obstructed, while a human's nature is part of a nature that cannot be obstructed, that is intelligent and just, since it allots to everything its fair share according to its worth: its time, its substance, its cause, its activity, and its circumstances. But do not look to find any single thing equal in all respects to another single thing; rather, compare the whole of one thing, taken together, with the whole of another.

You do not have the leisure to read. But you do have the leisure to curb arrogance; you have the leisure to rise above pleasure and pain; you have the leisure to rise above the love of fame, and not to be annoyed by foolish and ungrateful people, but even to care for them.
Let no one ever again hear you complaining about life at court, or about your own life.

Regret is a kind of self-reproach for having neglected something useful; but what is good must also be useful, and the truly good person should attend to it. Yet no such person would ever regret refusing a sensual pleasure. Therefore pleasure is neither good nor useful.
This thing, what is it in itself, in its own makeup? What is its substance and material? What is its causal nature? What is it doing in the world? And how long does it last?

When you rise from sleep reluctantly, remember that it is according to your makeup and to human nature to perform social acts, while sleeping is something you share even with irrational animals. And what is according to each individual's nature is more truly its own, more suited to it, and indeed more agreeable.
Constantly, and if possible at every impression that strikes your soul, apply to it the principles of physics, of ethics, and of logic.

Whatever person you meet, immediately say to yourself: What are this person's opinions about good and bad? For if they hold such and such views about pleasure and pain and their causes, about fame and disgrace, about death and life, then it will seem nothing surprising or strange to me when they act accordingly, and I will keep in mind that they are compelled to act this way.

Remember that just as it would be absurd to be surprised that a fig tree produces figs, so it is absurd to be surprised that the world produces the things it is bound to produce; and for a doctor and a ship's captain it would be a disgrace to be surprised that someone has a fever or that the wind is unfavorable.

Remember that changing your opinion and following someone who corrects your mistake is just as consistent with freedom as stubbornly persisting in your error. For the act is your own, carried out according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own understanding.

If something is within your own power, why do you do it? But if it is in another's power, whom do you blame, the atoms or the gods? Both are foolish. You must blame no one. For if you can, correct the cause; if you cannot do that, at least correct the thing itself; and if you cannot do even that, what good does it do you to find fault? Nothing should be done without purpose.

What has died does not fall out of the universe. If it remains here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into its proper parts, which are elements of the universe and of you. And these parts change too, and they do not complain.

Everything exists for some purpose: a horse, a vine. Why are you surprised? Even the sun will say, I exist for a purpose, and the rest of the gods will say the same. So what purpose do you exist for, to enjoy pleasure? See whether common sense allows this.

Nature has regard, in everything, no less for the ending than for the beginning and the continuance, just like a man throwing a ball into the air. What good is it for the ball to be thrown up, or what harm for it to come down, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to a bubble while it holds together, or what harm when it bursts? The same can be said of a flame.
Turn the body inside out and see what kind of thing it is; and what kind of thing it becomes when it has grown old, and when it is diseased.

Short-lived are both the one who praises and the one praised, the one who remembers and the one remembered, and all of this in a small corner of this part of the world; and even here people do not all agree, no, not even one person with themselves; and the whole earth too is but a point.
Attend to the matter before you, whether it is an opinion, an action, or a word.
You suffer this justly, because you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
Am I doing something? I do it for the good of mankind. Does something happen to me? I accept it and refer it to the gods and to the source of all things, from which everything that happens flows.
Just as bathing appears to you as oil, sweat, dirt, filthy water, all of it disgusting, so is every part of life and everything in it.

Lucilla saw Verus die, and then Lucilla died. Secunda saw Maximus die, and then Secunda died. Epitynchanus saw Diotimus die, and then Epitynchanus died. Antoninus saw Faustina die, and then Antoninus died. So it is with everything. Celer saw Hadrian die, and then Celer died. And those sharp-witted people, whether prophets or men puffed up with pride, where are they now? For instance the sharp-witted Charax, Demetrius the Platonist, Eudaemon, and anyone else like them? All short-lived, dead long ago. Some were not remembered even briefly; others have become the heroes of legends; and still others have vanished even from the legends. Remember, then, that this little composite thing, yourself, must either be dissolved, or your poor breath must be snuffed out, or be moved and placed elsewhere.

It is a satisfaction to a person to do the proper work of a human being. Now the proper work of a human being is to be kind to one's own kind, to disdain the urges of the senses, to form a sound judgment of plausible appearances, and to take a survey of the nature of the universe and of the things that happen in it.
There are three relationships: the first to the body that surrounds you; the second to the divine cause from which all things come to all; and the third to the people who live alongside you.

Pain is either an evil to the body, in which case let the body say what it thinks of it, or an evil to the soul; but it is in the soul's power to keep its own serenity and calm, and not to think pain an evil. For every judgment, impulse, desire, and aversion is within, and no evil rises that high.

Wipe out your imaginings by often saying to yourself: Right now it is in my power to let no wickedness be in this soul, nor desire, nor any disturbance at all; but looking at all things I see what their nature is, and I use each according to its value. Remember this power that nature has given you.
Speak in the senate and to every person, whoever they may be, appropriately and without affectation; use plain speech.

Augustus' court, his wife, daughter, descendants, ancestors, sister, Agrippa, his relatives, his close companions, his friends; Areius, Maecenas, his physicians, his sacrificing priests, the whole court is dead. Then turn to the rest, considering not the death of a single person but of a whole line, like the Pompeys; and that inscription on the tombs, The last of his line. Then consider what trouble those before them went through so as to leave a successor; and then that, of necessity, someone must be the last. Here again, consider the death of an entire line.

It is your duty to order your life well in every single act; and if every act does its duty as far as possible, be content; and no one can prevent each act from doing its duty. But some external thing will get in the way. Nothing will get in the way of your acting justly, soberly, and thoughtfully. But perhaps some other capacity for action will be hindered. Well then, by accepting the hindrance and being content to redirect your efforts to what is permitted, another opportunity for action is immediately set before you in place of the one that was blocked, one that fits the very ordering of life we are speaking of.
Receive wealth or prosperity without arrogance, and be ready to let it go.

If you ever saw a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head, lying somewhere apart from the rest of the body, that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as they can, who is not content with what happens, who cuts themselves off from others, or who does anything unsocial. Suppose you have detached yourself from the natural unity, for by nature you were made a part, but now you have cut yourself off; yet here is a beautiful provision: it is in your power to unite yourself again. God has granted this to no other part, that after being severed and cut off it may come together again. But consider the kindness with which he has honored humanity, for he has given a person the power not to be severed from the whole at all, and, once severed, to return, to be reunited, and to resume their place as a part.

Just as the nature of the universe has given every rational being all the other powers it has, so we have received this power from it too. For just as the universal nature turns and fixes in its appointed place everything that stands in its way and opposes it, making such things a part of itself, so too the rational being is able to turn every obstacle into material of its own and use it for whatever purposes it has in mind.

Do not disturb yourself by thinking of your whole life. Do not let your thoughts take in all at once the various troubles you may expect to befall you; instead, on each occasion ask yourself: What is there in this present thing that is unbearable and beyond enduring? You will be ashamed to admit there is anything. Next, remember that neither the future nor the past weighs on you, but only the present. And this shrinks to very little if you isolate it by itself, and rebuke your mind if it cannot hold out against even this.

Does Panthea or Pergamus now sit by the tomb of Verus? Does Chabrias or Diotimus sit by the tomb of Hadrian? That would be ridiculous. And even if they did sit there, would the dead be aware of it? And if the dead were aware, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would that make them immortal? Was it not in the order of destiny that these people too should first become old women and old men, and then die? And what would they do once these mourners were dead? All of this is foul-smelling stuff and blood in a bag.
If you can see clearly, look and judge wisely, says the philosopher.
In the makeup of the rational being I see no virtue that opposes justice; but I do see a virtue that opposes the love of pleasure, and that is self-control.

If you take away your opinion about what seems to give you pain, you yourself stand in perfect safety. Who is this self? The reason. But I am not just reason. Very well. Then let the reason not trouble itself. And if any other part of you suffers, let it hold its own opinion about itself.

Obstruction to the perceptions of the senses is an evil to the animal nature. Obstruction to its impulses is equally an evil to the animal nature. And something else likewise is an obstruction and an evil to the makeup of plants. So in the same way, whatever obstructs the intelligence is an evil to the intelligent nature. Now apply all of this to yourself. Does pain or sensual pleasure affect you? The senses will deal with that. Has some obstacle blocked you in your efforts toward a goal? If you were pursuing that goal unconditionally, with no reservation, then yes, this obstacle is an evil to you considered as a rational being. But if you take into account the usual course of things, you have not yet been harmed, or even hindered. As for the things that properly belong to the understanding, no other person is able to hinder them, for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor abuse can touch it in any way. Once it has been made a sphere, it remains a sphere.
It is not right that I should give myself pain, for I have never intentionally given pain even to another.

Different things delight different people; but my delight is to keep my ruling faculty sound, turning away from no person and from none of the things that happen to people, but looking at all of them and receiving them with welcoming eyes, and using everything according to its value.

See that you secure this present time for yourself, for those who chase fame after death do not consider that the people of later times will be exactly like these whom they cannot stand now, and both are mortal. And what is it to you, in any case, if these people of later times utter this or that sound, or hold this or that opinion about you?

Take me and cast me wherever you wish; for there too I will keep my divine part tranquil, that is, content, as long as it can feel and act in keeping with its proper makeup. Is this change of place a good enough reason for my soul to become unhappy and worse than it was, downcast, overstretched, shrinking, terrified? What could you find that would be a good enough reason for that?

Nothing can happen to a person that is not a human experience, nor to an ox that is not in keeping with the nature of an ox, nor to a vine that is not in keeping with the nature of a vine, nor to a stone that is not proper to a stone. So if what happens to each thing is both usual and natural, why should you complain? For the common nature brings nothing you cannot bear.

If you are pained by some external thing, it is not that thing that disturbs you, but your own judgment about it. And it is in your power to wipe out this judgment right now. But if something in your own disposition gives you pain, who prevents you from correcting your view? And even if you are pained because you are not doing something that seems right to you, why not act instead of complaining? But some insurmountable obstacle is in the way. Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done lies not with you. But it is not worth living if I cannot do this. Then depart from life contentedly, just as one dies who is in full activity, and at peace even with the things that obstruct them.

Remember that the ruling faculty is invincible when, gathered within itself, it is satisfied with itself, doing nothing it does not choose to do, even if its resistance comes from mere stubbornness. What, then, will it be like when it forms a judgment about something with the aid of reason and deliberation? For this reason a mind free from passions is a fortress, for a person has nothing more secure to flee to for refuge and to be forever unassailable. Whoever has not seen this is ignorant; but whoever has seen it and does not flee to this refuge is wretched.

Say nothing more to yourself than what the first appearances report. Suppose it is reported to you that a certain person speaks ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed, that has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. I do see that; but that he is in danger, I do not see. So always stay with the first appearances, and add nothing of your own from within, and then nothing happens to you. Or rather, add something, like a person who knows everything that happens in the world.

A cucumber is bitter? Throw it away. There are briars in the road? Turn aside from them. That is enough. Do not add, And why were such things made in the world? For you would be laughed at by someone who understands nature, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter or a shoemaker if you found fault with the shavings and offcuts you see in their workshop. And yet they have places to throw their shavings and offcuts, while the universal nature has no space outside herself; but the marvel of her art is that, though she has enclosed herself within limits, she changes into herself everything within her that seems to decay, grow old, and become useless, and from these very same things she makes other new things, so that she needs no material from outside and requires no place to dump what decays. She is content, then, with her own space, her own matter, and her own art.

Do not be sluggish in your actions, nor disorderly in your conversation, nor scattered in your thoughts; let there be no inner conflict in your soul, nor any outward gushing of it, and do not be so busy in life that you have no leisure.

Suppose people kill you, cut you to pieces, curse you. What can these things do to keep your mind from remaining pure, wise, sober, and just? For instance, if someone stood beside a clear, pure spring and cursed it, the spring would never stop sending up drinkable water; and if he threw clay or filth into it, it would quickly scatter and wash them away, and would not be polluted at all. How, then, will you possess a perpetual fountain, and not a mere well? By shaping yourself, hour by hour, toward freedom joined with contentment, simplicity, and modesty.

Whoever does not know what the world is does not know where they are. And whoever does not know the purpose for which the world exists does not know who they are, nor what the world is. But whoever has failed to grasp any one of these could not even say for what purpose they themselves exist. What, then, do you make of someone who chases the praise of those who applaud, of people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

Do you wish to be praised by someone who curses himself three times an hour? Would you wish to please someone who does not please himself? Does a person please himself who regrets nearly everything he does?

No longer let your breathing alone be in concert with the air that surrounds you; let your intelligence too now be in harmony with the intelligence that embraces all things. For the intelligent power is no less diffused through all parts and pervading all things, for the one who is willing to draw it in, than the power of the air is for the one who is able to breathe it.

In general, wickedness does no harm at all to the universe; and in particular, one person's wickedness does no harm to another. It is only harmful to the one who possesses it, who has it in their own power to be free of it the moment they choose.

To my own free will, my neighbor's free will is just as indifferent as their poor breath and flesh. For though we are made above all for one another's sake, still the ruling power of each of us has its own province; otherwise my neighbor's wickedness would be my harm, which God has not willed, so that my unhappiness need not depend on another.

The sun seems to be poured down and is indeed diffused in all directions, yet it is not poured away. For this diffusion is an extension; that is why its beams are called extensions, because they are extended. You can judge what kind of thing a ray is by looking at the sun's light passing through a narrow opening into a darkened room, for it is extended in a straight line, and is, as it were, divided when it meets any solid body that stands in its way and blocks the air beyond; yet there the light remains fixed and does not slide off or fall away. Such, then, should be the outpouring and diffusion of the understanding: in no way a pouring away, but an extension, making no violent or forceful collision with the obstacles in its path, and not falling down, but staying fixed and illuminating whatever receives it. For a body deprives itself of the light if it does not let it in.

Whoever fears death fears either the loss of sensation or a different kind of sensation. But if you will have no sensation, then you will feel no harm; and if you will acquire a different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living being and will not cease to live.
People exist for the sake of one another. So either teach them, or put up with them.
An arrow moves in one way, the mind in another. The mind, even when it exercises caution and when it is engaged in inquiry, moves no less straight ahead, toward its goal.
Enter into every person's ruling faculty, and also let every other person enter into yours.

Whoever acts unjustly acts irreverently toward the divine. Since universal nature made rational beings for one another's sake, to help each other as each deserves and never to harm one another, anyone who breaks her will is plainly guilty of irreverence toward the highest divinity. The liar, too, is guilty of irreverence toward that same divinity, for universal nature is the nature of all things that exist, and existing things are related to everything that comes into being. Furthermore, this universal nature is named truth, and is the first cause of all things that are true. So the man who lies on purpose is guilty of irreverence, since by deceiving he acts unjustly; and the man who lies without meaning to is also guilty, since he is out of step with universal nature and disturbs the order of things by fighting against the world's nature. For he does fight against it who, of his own accord, moves toward what is contrary to truth, since he had received from nature the powers which, by neglecting them, he can no longer use to tell falsehood from truth. And the man who chases pleasure as good and runs from pain as evil is likewise guilty of irreverence. For such a man must constantly find fault with universal nature, complaining that it hands out things to the bad and the good unfairly, because the bad so often enjoy pleasure and own the things that produce it, while the good get pain as their lot and the things that cause it. Again, the man who is afraid of pain will sometimes also be afraid of things that are bound to happen in the world, and that itself is irreverence. And the man who chases pleasure will not hold back from injustice, and that is plainly irreverence. Now toward those things to which universal nature is equally disposed—for it would not have made both unless it were equally disposed toward both—those who wish to follow nature should be of the same mind and equally disposed. So with regard to pain and pleasure, death and life, honor and dishonor, all of which universal nature uses equally, whoever is not equally disposed is clearly acting irreverently. And when I say universal nature uses them equally, I mean that they happen alike to those produced in continuous succession and to those who come after them, by virtue of a certain original movement of Providence, by which it moved from a certain beginning toward this ordering of things, having conceived certain principles of the things that were to be, and having determined the powers that produce beings and changes and such successions.

It would be a man's happiest fate to leave the human race without ever having tasted lying and hypocrisy and excess and pride. But to breathe out one's life when one has had quite enough of these things is, as the saying goes, the next best voyage. Have you decided to stay on with vice? Has experience not yet persuaded you to flee this plague? For the ruin of the understanding is a plague—far more so, in fact, than any corruption or change in the air around us. That corruption is a plague to animals insofar as they are animals; but this other one is a plague to human beings insofar as they are human.

Do not look down on death, but welcome it gladly, since it too is one of the things nature wills. For just as it is natural to be young and to grow old, to develop and reach maturity, to grow teeth and a beard and gray hair, to father children, to conceive, to give birth, and to go through all the other natural processes the seasons of your life bring, so too is dying. This, then, befits a thoughtful person: to be neither careless nor impatient nor scornful about death, but to wait for it as one of nature's operations. Just as you now wait for the time when the child will come out of your wife's womb, so be ready for the time when your soul will drop out of this shell. But if you also want a more ordinary kind of comfort, something to touch your heart, you will be best reconciled to death by looking at the things you are about to leave behind and the characters of the people your soul will no longer be mixed up with. For it is in no way right to be angry with people; instead, it is your duty to care for them and bear with them gently. And yet remember that you will not be departing from people who share your principles. For this is the only thing, if anything, that could pull us the other way and keep us attached to life—the chance to live among people who share our principles. But as it is, you see how much trouble comes from the discord of those who live together, so that you may well say: Come quickly, death, lest I too forget myself.
Whoever does wrong does wrong to himself. Whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.
A man often acts unjustly by not doing something, not only by doing something.
Your present judgment, grounded in understanding; your present conduct, directed toward the common good; your present attitude, content with everything that happens—that is enough.
Wipe out your impressions; rein in your desires; put out your appetites; keep the ruling faculty under its own control.

Among animals that have no reason, a single life is distributed; but among rational animals, a single intelligent soul is distributed—just as there is a single earth for all things of an earthly nature, and we all see by one light and breathe one air, all of us who have the power of sight and all who have life.

All things that share in something common to them move toward what is of their own kind. Everything earthy turns toward the earth; everything liquid flows together; everything of an airy kind does the same—so that they have to be kept apart by something, by the application of force. Fire, it is true, moves upward because of the elemental fire, yet it is so ready to catch with any fire here that even any fairly dry substance is easily set alight, because there is less mixed into it of what resists burning. In the same way, then, everything that shares in the common intelligent nature moves toward what is of its own kind—indeed moves even more strongly. For the more it surpasses all other things, the more ready it is to mingle with and fuse into what is akin to it. So among animals without reason we find swarms of bees, herds of cattle, the rearing of young birds, and, in a way, loves—for even in animals there are souls, and the power that draws them together is seen to assert itself to a higher degree than is ever observed in plants or stones or trees. But in rational animals there are political communities, friendships, families, and gatherings; and in wars, treaties and truces. And in things still higher, even though they are separated from one another, a kind of unity exists, as among the stars. Thus the ascent to a higher degree can produce sympathy even in things that are separated. See, then, what is happening now: only intelligent animals have forgotten this mutual longing and attraction, and in them alone the tendency to flow together is not seen. But still, though people try to avoid this union, they are caught and held by it, for their nature is too strong for them; and you will see what I mean if you simply observe. You will sooner find something earthy that touches no other earthy thing than a person wholly cut off from other people.

Both man and God and the universe bear fruit; each does so in its proper season. And if common usage has fixed the word 'fruit' especially to the vine and such things, that is nothing. Reason bears fruit both for all and for itself, and from it come other things of the same kind as reason itself.

If you can, correct those who do wrong by teaching them; but if you cannot, remember that forbearance was given to you for this very purpose. The gods, too, are forbearing toward such people; for certain ends they even help them obtain health, wealth, and reputation—that is how kind they are. And this is in your power as well; or tell me, who is stopping you?

Do your work not like someone miserable, nor like someone who wants to be pitied or admired; aim your will at one thing only—to set yourself in motion and to check yourself, as social reason requires.
Today I have escaped all trouble—or rather, I have thrown out all trouble, for it was not outside me but within, in my own judgments.
All things are the same: familiar from experience, short-lived in time, and worthless in substance. Everything now is exactly as it was in the days of those we have buried.
Things stand outside of us, by themselves and on their own, knowing nothing of themselves and passing no judgment. What is it, then, that judges about them? The ruling faculty.
For the rational social animal, evil and good lie not in being acted upon but in acting, just as his virtue and his vice lie not in being acted upon but in acting.
For the stone that has been thrown up, it is no evil to come down, nor was it any good to have been carried up.
Look inside men's guiding principles, and you will see what kind of judges you are afraid of, and what kind of judges they are of themselves.
All things are changing, and you yourself are in constant change and, in a way, in constant destruction—and so is the whole universe.
It is your duty to leave another man's wrongdoing right where it is.

The ending of an activity, the cessation of a movement or an opinion—their death, in a sense—is no evil. Turn your thoughts now to your own life: your life as a child, as a youth, as a grown man, in old age; for in each of these every change was a death. Was this anything to fear?
