Turn your thoughts now to your life under your grandfather, then your life under your mother, then your life under your father; and as you find many other differences and changes and endings, ask yourself: Is this anything to fear? In the same way, then, neither is the ending and cessation and change of your whole life anything to be afraid of.

Be quick to examine your own ruling faculty, and that of the universe, and that of your neighbor: your own, so that you may make it just; that of the universe, so that you may remember what you are a part of; and that of your neighbor, so that you may know whether he acted in ignorance or with knowledge, and may also consider that his ruling faculty is akin to your own.

Just as you yourself are a part of a social system, so let every act of yours be a part of social life. Any act of yours, then, that has no reference, directly or indirectly, to a social end tears your life apart, does not let it be one, and is of the nature of mutiny—just as, in a public assembly, a man who acts on his own stands apart from the general agreement.
The squabbles and games of little children, and feeble spirits carrying corpses about—such is everything; so that what is shown in the picture of the underworld strikes the eye more sharply.

Examine the quality of an object's form, separate it entirely from its material part, and then contemplate it; then work out the longest time that a thing of this particular form is naturally made to last.
You have endured endless troubles by not being content with your ruling faculty when it does the things it was constituted by nature to do. But enough of this.

When someone blames you or hates you, or when people say anything hurtful about you, go to their poor souls, get inside, and see what kind of men they are. You will discover that there is no reason to trouble yourself about what opinion they have of you. Even so, you must be well disposed toward them, for by nature they are friends. And the gods, too, help them in every way—by dreams, by signs—toward attaining the things they value.

The periodic movements of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age. Either the universal intelligence sets itself in motion for each separate effect—and if so, be content with what results from its activity; or it set itself in motion once, and everything else follows as a kind of consequence; or indivisible elements are the origin of all things. In short, if there is a god, all is well; and if chance rules, do not you too be ruled by it.

Soon the earth will cover us all; then the earth itself will change, and the things that result from that change will go on changing forever, and these again forever. For if a man reflects on these changes and transformations, following one another like wave after wave, and on how fast they come, he will look down on everything that perishes.

The universal cause is like a winter torrent: it sweeps everything along with it. But how worthless are all these poor people busy with political affairs and, as they imagine, playing the philosopher—all of them drivelers. Well then, man: do what nature now requires. Set yourself in motion, if it is in your power, and do not look around to see whether anyone notices; and do not wait for Plato's Republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes well, and consider such an outcome no small matter. For who can change men's opinions? And without a change of opinions, what is there but the slavery of men who groan while pretending to obey? Come now, tell me of Alexander and Philip and Demetrius of Phalerum. They themselves shall judge whether they found out what the common nature required and trained themselves accordingly. But if they acted like heroes in a tragedy, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest. Do not pull me aside into insolence and pride.

Look down from above on the countless herds of men, their countless ceremonies, their endlessly varied voyages through storms and calms, and the differences among those who are born, live together, and die. Consider, too, the lives lived by others long ago, the lives of those who will live after you, and the lives now lived among foreign nations; how many do not even know your name, and how many will soon forget it; how those who perhaps praise you now will very soon blame you; and that neither a name after death, nor reputation, nor anything else is of any value.

Let there be freedom from disturbance regarding the things that come from external causes; and let there be justice in the things done by your own internal cause—that is, let your movement and action end in this, in social acts, for this is in keeping with your nature.

You can clear away many of the useless things that disturb you, for they lie entirely in your own opinion; and you will then gain ample room for yourself by taking in the whole universe with your mind, contemplating the eternity of time, and observing how rapidly each separate thing changes—how short the span is from birth to dissolution, and how limitless the time before birth, and equally boundless the time after dissolution.

All that you see will quickly perish, and those who watched it dissolve will very soon perish too. And the man who dies at the most extreme old age will be brought to the same condition as the one who died too soon.

What are these men's guiding principles? With what kinds of things do they busy themselves? For what kinds of reasons do they love and honor? Imagine you can see their poor souls laid bare. When they suppose they do harm by blaming you or good by praising you, what a delusion!

Loss is nothing other than change. But universal nature delights in change, and in obedience to her all things are now done well, have been done so from eternity in the same form, and will be so for time without end. What, then, are you saying—that all things have been and always will be bad, and that no power was ever found among so many gods to set these things right, but that the world has been condemned to be bound in unceasing evil?

The rottenness of the matter that underlies everything! Water, dust, bones, filth; or again, marble—the calluses of the earth; gold and silver—mere sediment; clothing—just bits of hair; purple dye—just blood; and everything else is of the same kind. Even what is of the nature of breath is another thing of the same kind, changing from this to that.

Enough of this wretched life, and grumbling, and aping tricks. Why are you disturbed? What is there new in this? What unsettles you? Is it the form of the thing? Look at it. Or is it the matter? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing. So, toward the gods, become at last simpler and better. It makes no difference whether you examine these things for a hundred years or for three.
If a man has done wrong, the harm is his own. But perhaps he has not done wrong.

Either all things come from one intelligent source and fit together as in a single body—and then the part ought not to find fault with what is done for the good of the whole; or there are only atoms, and nothing but mixture and dispersion. Why, then, are you disturbed? Say to your ruling faculty: Are you dead? Are you corrupted? Are you playing the hypocrite? Have you become a beast? Do you herd and feed with the rest?

Either the gods have no power, or they have power. If they have no power, why do you pray to them? But if they have power, why not pray that they grant you the ability not to fear any of the things you fear, not to desire any of the things you desire, and not to grieve over anything—rather than praying that some of these things should or should not happen? For surely, if they can cooperate with men at all, they can cooperate toward these ends. But perhaps you will say: the gods have put these things in my own power. Well, then, is it not better to use what is in your power like a free man than to crave, in a slavish and groveling way, what is not in your power? And who told you that the gods do not help us even in the things that are in our power? Just start praying for such things, and you will see. One man prays: How may I manage to sleep with that woman? You pray: How may I not desire to sleep with her? Another prays: How may I be rid of this? You pray: How may I not desire to be rid of it? Another: How may I not lose my little son? You: How may I not be afraid to lose him? In short, turn your prayers this way, and see what comes of it.

Epicurus says: In my illness, my conversation was not about my bodily sufferings, nor, he says, did I talk of such things to those who visited me; instead I went on discussing the nature of things as before, keeping to this main point—how the mind, while sharing in such disturbances as go on in the poor flesh, can stay free of upheaval and keep hold of its own proper good. Nor, he says, did I give the doctors the chance to put on solemn looks, as if they were doing something great; my life went on well and happily. Do the same, then, that he did, both in sickness, if you fall sick, and in any other circumstance. For never to abandon philosophy whatever happens to us, and not to chatter idly with an ignorant man or one who knows nothing of nature, is a principle of all schools of philosophy; and so is being intent only on what you are doing now and on the instrument with which you do it.

When you are offended by someone's shameless behavior, ask yourself at once: Is it possible, then, for shameless men not to exist in the world? It is not possible. So do not demand the impossible. This man is simply one of those shameless men who must necessarily exist in the world. Keep the same considerations in mind in the case of the cheat, the faithless man, and everyone who does wrong in any way. For the moment you remind yourself that it is impossible for such men not to exist, you will be more kindly disposed toward each of them as an individual. It is useful, too, to notice right away, when the occasion arises, what virtue nature has given man to set against each kind of wrongdoing. As an antidote to the obtuse man she has given mildness, and against another kind of man some other power. And in every case it is possible for you to correct, by teaching, the man who has gone astray; for every man who errs misses his aim and has gone astray. Besides, how have you been harmed? You will find that none of those you are irritated with has done anything to make your mind worse; and what is bad and harmful to you has its foundation only in your mind. And what harm is done, or what is strange about it, if a man who has not been taught does the things of an untaught man? Consider whether you should not rather blame yourself for not expecting such a man to err in such a way. Your reason gave you the means to suppose he would likely make this mistake, and yet you forgot, and now you are amazed that he has erred. But most of all, when you blame a man as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For the fault is plainly your own—whether you trusted that a man with such a disposition would keep his promise, or whether, in doing him a kindness, you did not do it unconditionally, nor in such a way as to have received the whole profit from the very act. For what more do you want, when you have done a man a service? Is it not enough that you have done something in keeping with your nature—must you seek to be paid for it? That would be as if the eye demanded a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking. For just as these members were made for a particular purpose, and by working according to their own constitution get what is their own, so too man, formed by nature for acts of kindness, when he has done something kind or otherwise serving the common interest, has acted in keeping with his constitution and gets what is his own.

Will you ever, my soul, be good and simple and single and bare, more visible than the body that surrounds you? Will you ever taste a loving and contented disposition? Will you ever be full and lacking nothing, longing for nothing more, craving nothing—neither living thing nor object—for the enjoyment of pleasures? Will you stop craving more time in which to enjoy them longer, or a particular place, or a pleasant climate, or the company of people you can live with in harmony? Instead, will you be satisfied with your present condition, pleased with everything around you, and convince yourself that you have everything you need, that it all comes from the gods, that everything is well for you and will be well whatever they choose to give for the preservation of that perfect living being—the good and just and beautiful—which generates and holds all things together, and contains and embraces all things that dissolve so that other like things can be produced? Will you ever be such that you can live in community with gods and with people, never finding fault with them and never being condemned by them?

Observe what your nature requires insofar as you are governed by nature alone; then do it and accept it, provided your nature as a living being is not made worse by it. Next, observe what your nature requires insofar as you are a living being, and allow yourself all of that, provided your nature as a rational creature is not made worse by it. But a rational creature is by consequence also a social creature. So use these rules, and trouble yourself about nothing else.

Everything that happens either happens in a way you are naturally formed to bear, or in a way you are not. If it happens in a way you are formed to bear, do not complain, but bear it as you are formed to bear it. But if it happens in a way you are not formed to bear, still do not complain, for it will perish after it has consumed you. Remember, though, that you are naturally formed to bear everything that your own judgment can make endurable and tolerable, by thinking that it is either in your interest or your duty to do so.
If someone is mistaken, instruct him kindly and show him his error. But if you cannot, blame yourself—or not even yourself.
Whatever happens to you was prepared for you from all eternity; the chain of causes was, from eternity, spinning the thread of your existence and of everything that befalls it.

Whether the universe is a chance gathering of atoms, or a system governed by nature, let this first be settled: that I am a part of the whole which nature governs; and next, that I am in some way intimately related to the other parts of the same kind as myself. Remembering this, then, as a part I will be discontented with none of the things assigned to me out of the whole; for nothing that benefits the whole is harmful to the part. The whole contains nothing that is not for its own advantage. All natures share this principle, but the nature of the universe has this besides: that no external cause can ever compel it to generate anything harmful to itself. Remembering, then, that I am a part of such a whole, I will be content with everything that happens. And since I am intimately related to the parts of the same kind as myself, I will do nothing unsocial, but rather direct myself toward those who are akin to me, turn all my efforts toward the common good, and turn them away from the opposite. If things are done this way, life must flow on happily—just as you would expect the life of a citizen to be happy who pursues a course of action that benefits his fellow citizens and is content with whatever the state assigns to him.

The parts of the whole—everything, I mean, that is naturally contained in the universe—must necessarily perish; but understand this in the sense that they must undergo change. Now if change were by nature both an evil and a necessity for the parts, the whole could not continue in good condition, with its parts subject to change and so constituted as to perish in various ways. For did Nature herself deliberately set out to do evil to her own parts, making them subject to evil and bound to fall into it of necessity—or did such results come about without her knowing? Both suppositions are unbelievable. But suppose someone drops the term Nature as an active power and merely calls these things natural: even then it would be absurd to say that the parts of the whole are by nature subject to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though something were happening contrary to nature—especially since each thing dissolves into the very elements of which it is composed. For there is either a scattering of the elements out of which everything was compounded, or a change from the solid into the earthy and from the airy into the aerial, so that these parts are taken back into the universal reason—whether the universe is consumed by fire at fixed periods or renewed by eternal changes. And do not imagine that the solid and the airy parts of you have belonged to you since birth. All of it took on its growth only yesterday and the day before, so to speak, from the food you eat and the air you breathe. So it is this—what has grown—that changes, not what your mother brought forth. But suppose what your mother brought forth is closely bound up with that other part, the one that has the peculiar quality of changing: that is no objection at all to what I have said.

Once you have taken on these names—good, modest, truthful, rational, even-tempered, high-minded—take care never to exchange them for others; and if you ever lose them, return to them quickly. Remember that 'rational' was meant to signify a discriminating attention to each particular thing and a freedom from carelessness; that 'even-tempered' means the willing acceptance of whatever the common nature assigns to you; and that 'high-minded' means the elevation of the thinking part above the pleasant or painful sensations of the flesh, above that poor thing called fame, and above death and all such things. If, then, you keep hold of these names without craving to be called by them by others, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being what you have been until now—torn to pieces and defiled in such a life—is the mark of a very stupid man, far too fond of his life, like those half-devoured fighters in the arena who, though covered in wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until the next day, when they will be thrown out in the same state to the same claws and teeth. So plant yourself firmly in these few names, and if you are able to abide in them, abide as if you had been carried off to the Islands of the Blessed. But if you find that you are falling away from them and cannot keep your hold, then go bravely off into some corner where you can keep them—or even depart from life altogether, not in passion, but with simplicity and freedom and modesty, having at least done this one praiseworthy thing in your life, to have left it in this way. To help you remember these names, it will greatly help to remember the gods, and that they do not wish to be flattered but wish all reasonable beings to become like themselves; and to remember that what does the work of a fig tree is a fig tree, what does the work of a dog is a dog, what does the work of a bee is a bee, and what does the work of a man is a man.
"For there, indeed, man's life is easiest: no snow, no raging storm, no rain is there, but always Ocean sends up the gently breathing breezes of the West Wind to refresh mankind."

War, amazement, sluggishness, slavery, and the mime-shows of life will day by day wipe out those holy principles of yours—principles you picture without studying nature, and just as many that you neglect. Yet it is your duty to look at and to do everything in such a way that, at one and the same time, your power to deal with circumstances is brought to perfection, your contemplative faculty is exercised, and the confidence that comes from knowing each particular thing is kept—not displayed, but not concealed either. For when will you ever enjoy simplicity, when gravity, when the knowledge of each particular thing—what it is in substance, what place it holds in the universe, how long it is formed to last, what it is made of, to whom it can belong, and who can both give it and take it away?

A spider is proud when it catches a fly, one man when he catches a hare, another when he nets a little fish, another when he takes wild boars, another bears, and another Sarmatians. If you examine their principles, are these last not robbers too?

Acquire the contemplative way of seeing how all things change into one another; attend to it constantly and train yourself in this part of philosophy. Nothing is so apt to produce greatness of mind. Such a man has set aside the body, and seeing that he must—no one knows how soon—depart from among men and leave everything behind, he gives himself up entirely to acting justly in all that he does and to resigning himself, in everything else that happens, to the universal nature. As for what anyone may say or think about him or do against him, he never even gives it a thought, being content with these two things: to act justly in what he is now doing, and to be satisfied with what is now assigned to him. He lays aside all distracting and busy pursuits, and desires nothing else than to run the straight course according to the law, and by running the straight course to follow God.

What need is there for anxious suspicion, when it is in your power to inquire what ought to be done? If you see clearly, then go this way contentedly, without turning back; if you do not see clearly, then stop and take the best advice. But if other things stand in your way, go on as your powers allow, with careful consideration, holding to what seems just. For it is best to reach that goal, and if you fail, let your failure be in the attempt to reach it. The man who follows reason in all things is at once tranquil and active, cheerful and composed.
As soon as you wake from sleep, ask yourself whether it will make any difference to you if another person does what is just and right. It will make no difference.

You have not forgotten, I trust, that those who put on arrogant airs in dealing out their praise or blame to others are just what they are at bed and at table; you have not forgotten what they do, what they avoid, what they pursue, and how they steal and rob—not with hands and feet, but with their most valuable part, the part by which a man, when he chooses, produces fidelity, modesty, truth, law, and a good guiding spirit.

To Nature, who gives all things and takes them back, the man who is well taught and modest says: Give what you will; take back what you will. And he says this not out of pride, but in obedience, and well pleased with her.

Short is the little that remains of your life. Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether a man lives here or there, if he lives everywhere in the world as in a city. Let people see, let them know, a real man who lives according to nature. If they cannot endure him, let them kill him—for that is better than to live as men do.
No longer talk at all about the kind of man a good man ought to be. Be one.
Constantly contemplate the whole of time and the whole of substance, and consider that, in substance, every individual thing is but a grain of a fig, and in time but the single turn of a drill.
Look at everything that exists and observe that it is already breaking up and changing—a kind of decay or scattering—and that everything is so constituted by nature as to die.

Consider what men are when they are eating, sleeping, mating, relieving themselves, and so on. Then consider what kind of men they are when they are domineering and arrogant, or angry and scolding from their lofty positions. Yet a little while ago, to how many were they slaves, and for what things—and after a little while, consider the condition they will be in.
What the universal nature brings to each thing is for the good of that thing—and it is for its good at the very time nature brings it.

"The earth loves the rain," and "the majestic sky loves"—and the universe loves to bring about whatever is about to be. So I say to the universe: I love along with you. And is this not also why we say that this or that 'loves'—is wont—to come about?

Either you go on living here and have grown accustomed to it; or you are going away, and that was your own wish; or you are dying and have discharged your duty. Beyond these there is nothing. So take heart.

Always keep it clear to yourself that this patch of land is like any other, and that everything here is the same as on a mountaintop, or by the seashore, or wherever you choose to be. For you will find exactly what Plato says: dwelling within the walls of a city as in a shepherd's fold on a mountain.

What is my ruling faculty to me right now? What sort of thing am I now making it? For what purpose am I now using it? Is it empty of understanding? Is it cut loose and torn away from social life? Is it melted and mixed into this poor flesh, so that it moves along with it?

He who runs away from his master is a runaway slave. The law is our master, and whoever breaks the law is a runaway. So too is the man who is grieved or angry or afraid, because he is dissatisfied that something has been, is, or will be among the things appointed by the one who rules all things—and that ruler is Law, who assigns each man his due. The man, then, who fears or grieves or rages is a runaway.

A man deposits seed in a womb and goes away, and then another cause takes it up, works on it, and makes a child. What a thing from such material! Again, the child sends food down through its throat, and then another cause takes it and makes perception and movement, and in the end life and strength and all the rest—so many things, and so strange! Observe, then, the things produced in this hidden way, and see the power behind them, just as we see the power that carries things downward and upward—not with our eyes, yet no less plainly.

Constantly consider that all things, just as they are now, also were in time past, and that they will be the same again. Set before your eyes whole dramas and scenes of the same pattern, whatever you have learned from your own experience or from older history—for example, the whole court of Hadrian, the whole court of Antoninus, the whole court of Philip, Alexander, Croesus. All of those were just such dramas as we see now, only with different actors.
Imagine every man who is grieved or discontented at anything to be like a pig being sacrificed, kicking and squealing.

Like this pig, too, is the man who, lying on his bed in silence, laments the bonds in which we are held. And consider that to the rational creature alone is it given to follow willingly what happens; merely to follow is a necessity imposed on all.
On the occasion of each thing you do, pause and ask yourself whether death is a dreadful thing because it deprives you of this.

When you are offended at another man's fault, turn at once to yourself and reflect how you commit the same sort of error—for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and the like. By attending to this, you will quickly forget your anger, especially if you also consider that the man is under compulsion—for what else could he do? Or, if you are able, remove the compulsion from him.

When you have seen Satyron the Socratic, think of Eutyches or Hymen; when you have seen Euphrates, think of Eutychion or Silvanus; when you have seen Alciphron, think of Tropaeophorus; when you have seen Xenophon, think of Crito or Severus; and when you have looked at yourself, think of one of the other Caesars—and in every case do the same. Then let this thought come to mind: Where, then, are those men now? Nowhere, or nobody knows where. For in this way you will continually see human things as smoke and nothing at all, especially if you also reflect that what has once changed will never exist again in all the infinite span of time. And you—in how brief a stretch of time is your own existence? Why, then, are you not content to pass through this short time in an orderly way? What material and opportunity for your activity are you turning away from? For what else are all these things but exercises for the reason, once it has examined carefully and by close inquiry into their nature the things that happen in life? Persevere, then, until you have made these things your own—as a strengthened stomach makes all things its own, as a blazing fire turns whatever is thrown into it into flame and brightness.

Let it never be in any man's power to say truly of you that you are not simple or that you are not good; let whoever thinks anything of the kind about you be a liar. And this is entirely in your power. For who is there to stop you from being good and simple? Only resolve to live no longer if you cannot be such—for reason itself does not allow you to live if you are not.

In dealing with the material of our life, what can be done or said in the way most in keeping with reason? Whatever it may be, it is in your power to do it or to say it; so do not make excuses that you are hindered. You will not stop your lamenting until your mind reaches a state where doing the things in keeping with man's constitution, in whatever matter is set before you, is to you what luxury is to those who pursue pleasure. For a man ought to consider as an enjoyment everything it is in his power to do according to his own nature—and that is in his power everywhere. Now a cylinder is not given the power to move everywhere by its own motion, nor is water, nor fire, nor anything else governed by nature or by an irrational soul, for the things that check them and stand in their way are many. But intelligence and reason are able to make their way through everything that opposes them, in the manner they are formed by nature and as they choose. Set before your eyes this ease with which reason will be carried through all things, as fire moves upward, a stone downward, a cylinder down a slope—and seek nothing further. For all other obstacles either affect only the body, which is a dead thing, or—except through opinion and the yielding of reason itself—they do not crush us or do any harm at all; for if they did, the one who felt it would at once become bad. Indeed, in everything that has a certain constitution, whatever harm befalls it makes the thing that suffers it correspondingly worse; but in a man's case, he becomes better, if one may say so, and more worthy of praise by making right use of such accidents. And in the end, remember that nothing harms the man who is truly a citizen unless it harms the state, and nothing harms the state unless it harms law and order; and of the things called misfortunes, not one harms law. What, then, does not harm law harms neither state nor citizen.
To the man steeped in true principles, even the briefest reminder is enough, any common precept, to recall him to a life free from grief and fear. For example:
"Leaves—some the wind scatters on the ground—so is the race of men."

Leaves, too, are your children; leaves are those who cry out as if they deserved to be believed and bestow their praise, or on the contrary curse, or secretly blame and sneer; and leaves likewise are those who will receive and hand down a man's fame to later ages. For all such things "are produced in the season of spring," as the poet says; then the wind casts them down; then the forest brings forth other leaves in their place. A brief existence is common to all things, and yet you avoid and pursue them all as though they would last forever. In a little while you will close your eyes, and the man who carried you to your grave will soon be mourned by another.

A healthy eye ought to look at everything visible and not say, 'I want only green things'—for that is the condition of a diseased eye. Healthy hearing and smell ought to be ready to perceive all that can be heard and smelled. A healthy stomach ought to be toward all food just as a mill is toward all that it is made to grind. And so a healthy understanding ought to be ready for everything that happens; but the understanding that says, 'Let my dear children live, and let all men praise whatever I do,' is an eye that wants only green things, or teeth that want only soft food.

There is no man so fortunate that, when he is dying, there will not be some standing by who are pleased at what is about to happen. Suppose he was a good and wise man: will there not be at least someone to say to himself, 'Let us at last breathe freely, now that we are relieved of this schoolmaster? True, he was harsh to none of us, but I sensed that he silently condemned us'? That is what is said of a good man. But in our own case, how many other reasons are there why so many wish to be rid of us? Consider this, then, when you are dying, and you will depart more contentedly by reflecting thus: I am leaving a life in which even my own companions—those for whom I strove so much, prayed, and cared—themselves wish me gone, hoping perhaps to gain some small advantage by it. Why, then, should a man cling to a longer stay here? Yet do not on that account leave them any less kindly disposed; keep your own character, friendly and benevolent and gentle, and do not depart as if you were being torn away. Rather, just as when a man dies a quiet death the poor soul is easily separated from the body, so too should your departure from men be. For nature bound you to them and joined you with them—and now she dissolves the union. I am separated as from kinsmen, yet not dragged off resisting, but going without compulsion; for this too is one of the things in keeping with nature.
Train yourself, as much as you can, whenever anyone does anything, to ask yourself: For what purpose is this man doing this? But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.

Remember that what pulls the strings is the thing hidden within: this is the power of persuasion, this is life, this, one might say, is the man. In picturing yourself, never include the vessel that surrounds you and these instruments attached to it. For they are like an axe, differing only in that they have grown onto the body. Indeed, these parts are of no more use without the cause that moves and checks them than a weaver's shuttle is without the weaver, a pen without the writer, or a whip without the driver.

These are the properties of the rational soul: it sees itself, analyzes itself, and makes itself whatever it chooses. The fruit it bears, it enjoys itself—whereas the fruit of plants, and what corresponds to fruit in animals, others enjoy. It reaches its own end wherever the limit of life happens to fall. It is not like a dance or a play or anything of that kind, where the whole performance is left incomplete if something cuts it short; rather, in every part, and wherever it may be stopped, it makes whatever was set before it full and complete, so that it can say, "I have what is my own." What is more, it ranges over the whole universe and the empty space surrounding it, surveys its shape, reaches out into the infinity of time, and embraces and grasps the periodic renewal of all things. It understands that those who come after us will see nothing new, and that those before us saw nothing more; in a sense, anyone forty years old who has any understanding at all has already seen, through the uniformity that prevails, everything that has been and everything that will be. This too is a property of the rational soul: love of your neighbor, and truth, and modesty, and valuing nothing more than itself—which is also a property of Law. So right reason and the reason of justice are no different at all.

You will set little value on a pleasing song, or on dancing, or on the wrestling match, if you break the melody of the voice down into its separate sounds and ask yourself, about each one, whether this is what has mastered you—for shame will keep you from admitting it. Do the same with dancing, taking each movement and posture separately, and the same with the wrestling match. In all things, then—except virtue and the acts of virtue—remember to break them down into their parts, and by this dividing learn to value them little. Apply this rule to your whole life as well.

What a soul it is that is ready, the moment it must be separated from the body, to be extinguished, or scattered, or to go on existing—but ready in a way that comes from its own considered judgment, not from sheer stubbornness, as with the Christians, but with deliberation and dignity, and in a way that could persuade another, without any theatrical display.
Have I done something for the common good? Then I have had my reward. Keep this always before your mind, and never stop doing such good.
What is your craft? To be good. And how is that done well, except through general principles—some about the nature of the universe, others about the proper makeup of a human being?

Tragedies were first brought onto the stage to remind people of the things that happen to them, and that it is according to nature for such things to happen, and that if you enjoy watching them on the stage you should not be distressed when they take place on the larger stage of life. For you see that these things must turn out this way, and that even those who cry out "O Cithaeron!" still have to bear them. And indeed the dramatists do say some things well, especially lines like this one: "If the gods neglect me and my children, this too has its reason." And again: "We must not chafe and fret at what happens." And: "Reap life's harvest like a ripe ear of wheat." And other things of the same kind. After tragedy came the old comedy, with its blunt freedom of speech, useful by its very plainness in reminding people to beware of arrogance—which is also why Diogenes drew on these writers. As for the middle comedy that came next, look at what it was; and consider, too, what the new comedy was introduced for, which gradually sank into mere mimicry and stage trickery. Everyone knows that even these writers say some good things—but the whole aim of such poetry and drama, what does it ultimately come to?
How plainly it appears that there is no condition of life so well suited to philosophy as this one you happen to be in right now.

A branch cut off from the branch next to it is necessarily cut off from the whole tree as well. In the same way, a person cut off from another person has fallen away from the whole community. Now a branch is cut off by someone else, but a person cuts himself off from his neighbor by his own act, when he hates him and turns away from him—not realizing that at the same time he has cut himself off from the whole social system. Yet he still has this gift from Zeus, who framed society: it is in our power to grow back onto what is near us and to become once more a part that helps make up the whole. But if this kind of separation happens often, it becomes hard for the part that detaches itself to be brought back into unity and restored to its former state. In the end, the branch that grew with the tree from the start and shared one life with it is not the same as one that is cut off and then grafted back on. As the gardeners put it, such a branch grows together with the rest of the tree, but it does not share the same mind with it.

Just as those who try to block your way when you are acting according to right reason cannot turn you aside from your proper course, do not let them drive you from your goodwill toward them either. Stand guard equally on both fronts: not only in steadiness of judgment and action, but also in gentleness toward those who try to hinder you or otherwise give you trouble. For it is a weakness to be irritated at them, just as it is a weakness to be turned from your action or to give way through fear. Both are deserters from their post—the one who acts from fear, and the one who becomes estranged from a man who is by nature his kinsman and friend.

No nature is inferior to art, for the arts imitate the natures of things. And if that is so, then the most perfect and all-embracing of natures cannot fall short of the skill of art. Now all the arts make lesser things for the sake of greater ones; so the universal nature does the same. And from this, in fact, comes the origin of justice, and on justice the other virtues are founded—for justice will not be honored if we care about indifferent things, or if we are easily deceived, careless, and changeable.

If the things whose pursuit and avoidance disturb you do not come to you, still, in a way, you go to them. Let your judgment about them be at rest, then, and they will stay quiet, and you will not be seen either chasing or fleeing anything.

The soul keeps its spherical form when it is neither stretched out toward any object, nor drawn inward, nor scattered, nor collapsed inward, but is lit by a light through which it sees the truth—the truth of all things and the truth that is in itself.

Suppose someone despises me. That is his concern. Mine is to make sure I am not caught doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Suppose someone hates me. That too is his concern. I will be mild and kindly toward everyone, ready even to show that man his mistake—not in reproach, nor as a show of my own patience, but honestly and nobly, like the great Phocion (unless even he was only pretending). For the inner self ought to be like this, and a man ought to be seen by the gods neither dissatisfied with anything nor complaining. What harm can it be to you, if you are now doing what suits your own nature and are content with what at this moment suits the nature of the universe—you, a human being stationed at your post so that the common good may somehow be served?
People look down on one another and flatter one another; they want to rise above one another, and yet they grovel before one another.

How false and insincere is the man who says, "I have made up my mind to deal honestly with you!" What are you doing, man? There is no need to announce it. It will show itself soon enough in your actions. The truth ought to be plainly written on your forehead. A person's character shows at once in his eyes, just as someone who is loved reads everything in the eyes of those who love him. A man who is honest and good ought to be like a man with a strong smell, so that anyone who comes near him cannot help noticing it whether he wants to or not. But a put-on simplicity is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more disgraceful than a wolfish, false friendship. Avoid that above all. The good, simple, kindly man shows all this in his eyes; there is no mistaking it.

As for living in the best way, this power lies in the soul, provided it stays indifferent to things that are indifferent. And it will stay indifferent if it looks at each of these things separately and all together, and remembers that none of them forces an opinion of itself on us or comes to us; they stay still and unmoving, and it is we ourselves who form the judgments about them and, so to speak, write them into ourselves—when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, if such judgments have slipped in unnoticed, to wipe them out. Remember too that such attention is needed only for a short while, and then life will be over. Besides, what is so hard about doing this? If these things are according to nature, take joy in them and they will come easily; but if they are contrary to nature, look for what agrees with your own nature and strive toward that, even if it brings no reputation—for every man is allowed to seek his own good.
Consider where each thing comes from, what it is made of, what it changes into, and what kind of thing it will be once it has changed—and that it will take no harm at all.

If anyone has wronged you, consider this first: what is my relation to other people? We are made for one another; and, in another sense, I was made to be set over them, as a ram over the flock or a bull over the herd. But examine the matter from first principles, this way: if all things are not mere atoms, then it is nature that orders everything; and if that is so, the lesser things exist for the sake of the greater, and these for the sake of one another.
Second, consider what kind of men they are at the table, in bed, and so on; and especially what compulsions of opinion they are under; and as for their acts, with what pride they do what they do.

Third, that if people do rightly what they do, we have no reason to be displeased; and if they do wrong, it is plainly against their will and out of ignorance. For just as every soul is robbed of the truth against its will, so too it is robbed against its will of the power to treat each person as he deserves. That is why people are stung when they are called unjust, ungrateful, greedy—in a word, wrongdoers toward their neighbors.

Fourth, consider that you too do many things wrong, and that you are a man like the rest. And even if you do hold back from certain faults, you still have the disposition to commit them, and if you refrain it is only through cowardice, or concern for your reputation, or some such mean motive.

Fifth, consider that you do not even really know whether people are doing wrong or not, for many things are done with some reference to circumstances. In short, a man must learn a great deal before he can judge another man's actions correctly.
Sixth, consider, when you are very vexed or grieved, that a man's life is only a moment, and that in a short time we are all laid out dead.

Seventh, that it is not people's acts that disturb us, for those acts rest on their own ruling principles; it is our own opinions that disturb us. Take away these opinions, then—resolve to drop your judgment that the act is something dreadful—and your anger is gone. And how do I take away these opinions? By reflecting that no wrong done by another brings shame on me. For unless what is shameful were the only bad thing, I too would necessarily do many wrongs and become a robber and everything else.
Eighth, consider how much more pain is caused us by the anger and vexation over such acts than by the acts themselves that we are angry and vexed about.

Ninth, consider that a good disposition is unconquerable, provided it is genuine and not an affected smile and play-acting. For what can even the most violent man do to you if you go on being kind toward him, and, as the chance arises, gently advise him and calmly correct his errors at the very moment he is trying to harm you—saying, "Not so, my child; we were made by nature for something else. You will certainly not injure me, but you are injuring yourself, my child." And show him, with gentle tact and by general principles, that this is so—that not even bees behave as he does, nor any animals that nature has made to live in groups. And you must do this without any double meaning and without reproach, but affectionately and with no bitterness in your soul—not as if you were lecturing him, nor so that any bystander might admire you, but either when he is alone, or, if others are present, gently take him aside.

Remember these nine rules as if you had received them as a gift from the Muses, and begin at last to be a man while you are alive. But you must equally avoid flattering people and being vexed at them, for both are unsocial and lead to harm. And keep this truth before you when anger flares up: that to be moved by passion is not manly, whereas mildness and gentleness, as they are more in keeping with human nature, are also more manly. The man who has these qualities has strength, sinew, and courage—not the man given to fits of passion and discontent. For the nearer a man's mind comes to freedom from passion, the nearer it comes to strength; and just as pain is a mark of weakness, so is anger. The man who gives way to pain and the man who gives way to anger are both wounded, and both have surrendered.

And if you will, take a tenth gift as well, from the leader of the Muses, Apollo: that to expect bad men not to do wrong is madness, for that is to want the impossible. But to allow them to behave so toward others while expecting them not to wrong you is irrational and tyrannical.

There are four chief errors of the ruling faculty to be constantly on guard against; when you have caught them, wipe them out, saying in each case: "This thought is not necessary." "This one tends to destroy the bonds of society." "What you are about to say does not come from your real thoughts"—and you should count it among the most absurd of things for a man not to speak from his real thoughts. And the fourth is when you reproach yourself, for that is proof that the diviner part within you has been overpowered and is yielding to the lower, perishable part—the body—and to its coarse pleasures.

The airy part in you and all the fiery parts mixed into you, though by nature they tend upward, still obey the arrangement of the universe and are held down here in the compound mass of the body. And the earthy and watery parts in you, though their tendency is downward, are still raised up and kept in a position that is not their natural one. In this way the elements obey the whole: once fixed in some place, they stay there by necessity until the universe again sounds the signal for their dissolution. Is it not strange, then, that only your intelligent part should be disobedient and discontented with its place? And yet nothing is forced on it but what agrees with its own nature; still it does not submit, but is carried the opposite way. For the movement toward injustice, intemperance, anger, grief, and fear is nothing but the act of one who departs from nature. And when the ruling faculty is discontented with anything that happens, it too is deserting its post, for it was made for piety and reverence toward the gods no less than for justice. These qualities, too, are included under the general heading of contentment with the way things are constituted—indeed, they come before acts of justice.

A man who does not have one and the same aim throughout his life cannot be one and the same person throughout his life. But what I have said is not enough unless this is added too: what that aim ought to be. For just as people do not hold the same view about all the things commonly thought to be good, but only about certain ones—those that concern the common interest—so too the aim we set before ourselves should be of a common, social, and civic kind. The man who directs all his efforts toward this aim will make all his actions of one piece, and so he will always be the same.
Think of the country mouse and the town mouse, and of the alarm and panic of the town mouse.
Socrates used to call the opinions of the crowd "Lamiae"—bogeymen to frighten children.
At their public spectacles the Spartans used to set out seats in the shade for strangers, while they themselves sat down wherever they could.
Socrates made his excuses to Perdiccas for not visiting him, saying it was because he did not want to perish by the worst of all deaths—that is, to receive a favor and then be unable to return it.
In the writings of the Ephesians there was this precept: to keep thinking of someone from earlier times who practiced virtue.

The Pythagoreans tell us to look up at the heavens in the morning, so that we may be reminded of those bodies that forever do the same things in the same way as they go about their work, and reminded too of their purity and their nakedness—for there is no veil over a star.

Consider what a man Socrates was, when he wrapped himself in a skin after Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out, and what he said to the friends who were ashamed of him and shrank back when they saw him dressed like that.
Neither in writing nor in reading will you be able to set down rules for others before you have first learned to obey rules yourself. And this is far more true in life.
You are a slave: free speech is not for you.
"And my heart laughed within me."
"And they will curse virtue, speaking harsh words."
To look for a fig in winter is a madman's act; and so is the man who looks for his child when it is no longer permitted.

When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, "Perhaps tomorrow you will die." But those are words of bad omen. "No word is of bad omen," said Epictetus, "that names a work of nature; or, if it is, then it is also of bad omen to speak of the ears of corn being reaped."
The unripe grape, the ripe cluster, the dried raisin—all are changes, not into nothing, but into something that does not yet exist.
No one can rob us of our free will.

Epictetus also said that a man must work out an art, or set of rules, for giving his assent; and in his impulses to act he must take care that they suit the circumstances, serve the common interest, and match the worth of their object; and as for sensual desire, he should keep away from it altogether; and as for aversion, he should not direct it at anything that is not in our power.
The dispute, then, he said, is not about some trivial matter, but about whether we are sane or mad.

Socrates used to ask: What do you want—the souls of rational beings, or of irrational ones? Of rational ones. Of what kind of rational beings—sound or unsound? Sound. Then why do you not look for them? Because we already have them. Then why do you fight and quarrel?

Everything you hope to reach by some roundabout path, you can have right now, if you stop denying it to yourself. And this means: take no notice of all the past, trust the future to providence, and direct only the present in line with piety and justice. In line with piety, so that you are content with the lot assigned to you, for nature designed it for you and you for it. In line with justice, so that you always speak the truth freely and without disguise, and do what accords with the law and with the worth of each person. Don't let yourself be held back by another's wickedness, nor by opinion, nor by anyone's words, nor even by the sensations of the poor flesh that has grown around you, for that passive part can look after itself. If then, whenever the time comes that you are near your departure, you set everything else aside and respect only your ruling faculty and the divinity within you, and if you are afraid not because you must someday stop living, but rather that you may never have begun to live according to nature, then you will be a person worthy of the universe that produced you. You will no longer be a stranger in your own homeland, no longer astonished at things that happen daily as if they were unexpected, and no longer dependent on this or that.

God sees the minds of all people stripped bare of their material clothing, their husk, their impurities. For with his intellectual part alone he touches only the intelligence that has flowed and been derived from himself into these bodies. And if you train yourself to do the same, you will rid yourself of much trouble. For someone who pays no attention to the poor flesh that wraps him will surely not bother himself chasing after clothing, housing, fame, and other such externals and show.

There are three things you are made of: a little body, a little breath, and intelligence. The first two are yours only in the sense that it is your duty to take care of them, but the third alone is truly yours. So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your understanding, whatever others do or say, and whatever you yourself have done or said, and whatever future things trouble you because they might happen, and whatever in the body that wraps you or in the breath naturally joined to it is attached to you independent of your will, and whatever the external swirling current whirls around you, so that your intellectual power, exempt from the things of fate, can live pure and free by itself, doing what is just, accepting what happens, and speaking the truth; if you separate, I say, from this ruling faculty the things that cling to it through the impressions of the senses, and the things of time to come and time past, and make yourself like Empedocles' sphere, "all round, and resting in its own joyous repose"; and if you strive to live only what is really your life, that is, the present, then you will be able to spend whatever portion of life remains to you, right up to your death, free from disturbance, nobly, and obedient to the god that is within you.

I have often wondered how it is that every person loves himself more than everyone else, yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinions of others. If a god or a wise teacher were to appear and order a man to think nothing and plan nothing that he would not say aloud the moment he conceived it, he could not bear it even for a single day. So much more do we respect what our neighbors will think of us than what we think of ourselves.

How can it be that the gods, having arranged everything well and kindly for humankind, overlooked this one thing: that some people, and very good ones, people who have had the closest communion with the divine and through pious acts and religious observance have been most intimate with it, once they have died should never exist again but be completely snuffed out? But if this is so, rest assured that if it ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have made it so. For if it were just, it would also be possible; and if it were according to nature, nature would have arranged it that way. But because it is not so, if in fact it is not so, then be convinced that it ought not to have been so. For you can see for yourself that in raising this question you are arguing with the Deity, and we would not argue with the gods this way unless they were utterly excellent and just; and if they are, they would not have allowed anything in the ordering of the universe to be unjustly or irrationally neglected.

Practice yourself even in the things you despair of accomplishing. For even the left hand, useless at everything else for lack of practice, grips the bridle more firmly than the right, because it has been practiced at this.

Consider what condition a person should be in, in both body and soul, when death overtakes him; and consider the shortness of life, the boundless abyss of time past and to come, and the feebleness of all matter.

Contemplate the formative principles of things stripped of their coverings; the purposes behind actions; consider what pain is, what pleasure is, and death, and fame; consider that each person is the cause of his own unease, that no one is hindered by another, and that everything is a matter of opinion.

In applying your principles, be like the all-in fighter, not the swordsman; for the swordsman drops the sword he uses and is killed, but the fighter always has his hand and need do nothing but use it.
See things as they are in themselves, dividing them into matter, form, and purpose.
What power a person has to do nothing except what God will approve, and to accept everything God may give him.

As for what happens according to nature, we should blame neither the gods, since they do nothing wrong either willingly or unwillingly, nor other people, since they do nothing wrong except unwillingly. So we should blame no one.
How ridiculous, and what a stranger to life, is the person who is surprised at anything that happens in it.

Either there is a fated necessity and an unbreakable order, or a kind providence, or a confusion without purpose and without anyone directing it. If there is an unbreakable necessity, why do you resist? But if there is a providence that allows itself to be won over, make yourself worthy of the divinity's help. And if there is a confusion with no one governing it, be content that in such a storm you have within yourself a certain ruling intelligence. And even if the storm sweeps you away, let it sweep away the poor flesh, the poor breath, and everything else; for the intelligence, at least, it will not sweep away.
Does the light of the lamp shine without losing its brightness until it is put out? And shall the truth, the justice, and the self-control within you be put out before your death?

When someone appears to have done wrong, ask: how do I really know this was a wrongful act? And even if he did wrong, how do I know he has not already condemned himself, so that this is like clawing his own face? Consider that wanting a bad man not to do wrong is like wanting the fig tree not to yield juice in its figs, or babies not to cry, or the horse not to neigh, or anything else that must happen of necessity. For what else can a man do who has such a character? If this irritates you, then cure his disposition.
If it is not right, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.

In everything, always observe what the thing is that produces an impression on you, and break it down by dividing it into its form, its matter, its purpose, and the span of time within which it must end.

Realize at last that you have within you something better and more divine than the things that stir your passions and pull you about like a puppet on strings. What is in my mind right now? Is it fear, suspicion, desire, or something of the kind?
First, do nothing aimlessly or without a purpose. Second, let your actions aim at nothing but the good of the community.

Consider that before long you will be no one and nowhere, and none of the things you now see will exist, nor any of the people now living. For all things are made by nature to change, to be transformed, and to perish, so that other things may come into being in continuous succession.

Consider that everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power. So take away your opinion whenever you choose, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you will find calm, everything steady, a waveless bay.

Any activity, whatever it is, when it ends at its proper time suffers no harm by ending; nor does the one who performed it suffer any harm for the reason that the act has ended. In the same way, the whole made up of all our acts, which is our life, if it ends at its proper time suffers no harm by ending; nor is the one who brings this series to a close at the proper time badly treated. The proper time and the limit are fixed by nature, sometimes by a person's own nature, as in old age, but always by the universal nature, by the changing of whose parts the whole universe stays ever young and perfect. And whatever is useful to the whole is always good and timely. So the end of life is no evil for anyone, since it is not shameful, being beyond our will and not opposed to the common good; rather it is good, since it is timely and useful and fitting to the whole. For in this way too a person is moved by the Deity, when he is moved as the Deity is moved, and moved in his mind toward the same end.

Keep these three principles ready. First, in what you do, do nothing aimlessly or otherwise than justice herself would act; and as for what may come to you from outside, consider that it happens either by chance or by providence, and you must neither blame chance nor accuse providence. Second, consider what each being is from its seed until it receives a soul, and from receiving a soul until it gives that soul back, and what each is composed of and into what it dissolves. Third, that if you were suddenly lifted high above the earth and looked down on human affairs and saw how varied they are, and at the same time saw at a glance the great number of beings who dwell all around in the air and the heavens, you would see, however often you were lifted up, the very same things: the same forms, the same brief duration. Are these things to be proud of?
Throw away opinion, and you are saved. Who, then, stops you from throwing it away?

When you are troubled about anything, you have forgotten this: that all things happen according to the universal nature. And you have forgotten that another person's wrongful act is nothing to you. And you have forgotten that everything that happens always happened this way, will happen this way, and is happening this way everywhere right now. And you have forgotten how close the kinship is between one person and the whole human race, for it is a community not of a little blood or seed but of intelligence. And you have forgotten that each person's intelligence is a god and an outflow of the Deity; and that nothing is truly a person's own, but that his child, his body, and his very soul came from the Deity; and that everything is opinion; and, lastly, that every person lives only the present moment, and loses only this.

Constantly call to mind those who have complained loudly about something, those who were most conspicuous for the greatest fame, misfortunes, feuds, or fortunes of any kind, and then ask: where are they all now? Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale. Bring to mind too every example of this sort: how Fabius Catellinus lived on his country estate, Lucius Lupus in his gardens, Stertinius at Baiae, Tiberius at Capri, and Velius Rufus, and in short the eager pursuit of anything joined with pride, and how worthless everything is that people violently strain after, and how much more philosophical it is for a person, in the opportunities given to him, to show himself just, self-controlled, and obedient to the gods, and to do this in all simplicity; for the pride that prides itself on having no pride is the most unbearable pride of all.

To those who ask, Where have you seen the gods, or how do you grasp that they exist, that you worship them? I answer, first, that they can be seen even with the eyes; and second, that I have never seen even my own soul, and yet I honor it. So with the gods too: from what I constantly experience of their power, I grasp that they exist, and I revere them.

The safety of life lies in this: to examine everything thoroughly, what it is in itself, what its matter is, what its form; and with all your soul to do justice and to speak the truth. What is left, except to enjoy life by joining one good thing to another so closely as to leave not even the smallest gap between them?

There is one light of the sun, though it is broken up by walls, mountains, and countless other things. There is one common substance, though it is distributed among countless bodies, each with its own qualities. There is one soul, though it is distributed among countless natures and individual forms. There is one intelligent soul, though it seems to be divided. Now of the things just mentioned, the other parts, such as air and matter, are without sensation and have no fellowship with one another, and yet even these the intelligent principle holds together, along with their tendency toward the same center. But intellect in a special way tends toward what is akin to it, joins with it, and its feeling for community is not broken off.

What do you wish for? To go on existing? Well then, do you wish to have sensation, movement, growth, and then to stop growing, to use your speech, to think? Which of all these seems to you worth desiring? But if it is easy to set little value on all of them, then turn to what remains, which is to follow reason and God. Yet it is inconsistent with honoring reason and God to be troubled that death will deprive you of those other things.

How small a part of boundless, unfathomable time is allotted to each of us, for it is soon swallowed up in eternity. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the universal soul; and on what a tiny clod of the whole earth you creep. Reflecting on all this, consider nothing great except to act as your nature leads you and to endure what the common nature brings.
How does your ruling faculty make use of itself? Everything depends on this. Everything else, whether it lies within your will or not, is only lifeless ashes and smoke.
This reflection is best suited to move us to scorn death: that even those who think pleasure a good and pain an evil have still despised it.

For the person to whom only what comes in due season is good, to whom it makes no difference whether he has done more acts or fewer in accord with right reason, to whom it makes no difference whether he contemplates the world for a longer or a shorter time, for this person death too is not a terrible thing.

Man, you have been a citizen in this great city, the world; what does it matter to you whether for five years or three? For what accords with its laws is just for all alike. Where is the hardship, then, if you are sent out of the city not by a tyrant or an unjust judge, but by nature, who brought you into it, just as a director who hired an actor dismisses him from the stage? "But I have not finished the five acts, only three." You are right, but in life three acts are the whole play; for the one who once caused its composition and now causes its dissolution decides what counts as a complete drama, and you are the cause of neither. So depart contented, for the one who releases you is also contented.
